utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we continue to hear the evidence of the witness, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the admission of 65 ter 1D7846 discussed on the 7th of March, 2013, during the testimony of Mane Djuric and 65 ter 1D855 discussed on the 11th of March, 2013, during the testimony of Tomislav Puhalac. 65 ter 1D7846 is a statement given by Fikret Muminovic to the Milici public security station on the 4th of April 1992 and 65 ter 1D855 is a statement given by Senad Memic to officials of the MUP of Republika Srpska on the 14th of April, 1992. In light of the parties' submissions on the admission of these two documents, the Chamber considers it necessary to recall its practice, that third party statements not prepared for the purpose of current criminal proceedings can be admitted only if they are commented upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand. Both of these two documents fall into this category. More specifically, the Chamber is satisfied that Djuric sufficiently commented on 65 ter 1D7846 for the purpose of admission. The Chamber will thus MFI 1D7846 pending receipt of its English translation. In relation to 1D855, the Chamber recalls that the accused already sought its admission on two previous occasions. First, during the testimony of Robert Donia on the 9th of June, 2010, and, second, during the testimony of Momcilo Mandic, on the 8th of July, 2010. On both of these occasions, the Chamber denied admission. On the 11th of March, 2013, Puhalac provided further details as to the source of the document and gave his position as to the accuracy of its contents. The Chamber is therefore satisfied that 1D855 may now be admitted. The Registrar will assign the relevant exhibit numbers in due course. That said, shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 1D7846 will be MFI'd D3120; and 65 ter number 1D855 will be Exhibit D3121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pleas make yourself comfortable. We'll continue with your cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, when we left --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please speak up a little? I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our usher will assist you. Mr. Tesic, do you hear me well, now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, when we left off, I was beginning to talk about paragraph 41 of your statement, which -- your Defence statement, where you state: "On the night of 13 or 14 July I saw several buses loaded with Muslims in the town of Bratunac. At that time I thought these people were from Potocari and could not be transported at night. There were no soldiers in the city," et cetera. "The next day I learned that there were several Muslim corpses in the Vuk Karadzic primary school." Now, you agree with me on the 13th of July in Bratunac, these days you described yesterday as critical, there were buses and trucks of captured and separated Muslim men -- men, all over the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say specifically that this was throughout Bratunac. I did see buses outside the municipal buildings, some three, four, or five of them, and in a small street leading to the elementary school. Now, how many buses exactly there were, I don't know, because, in fact, I only saw them in the evening, and again I can't recall whether it was the 13th or the 14th precisely. Now, I was in my office and from there I could see -- you could see the buses, if you look out the window, but I could also smell the exhaust coming out of the buses because their engines were on so that's how I actually noticed them. I went down to the entrance to the building and I saw that these buses were full of people. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So is that your testimony, that you didn't leave the office on the 13th? You only saw what you could see from the front of your municipality building in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't walk about in the town to see something in particular. What I saw is mainly what you saw that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was -- you were staying in your office because, as you said in your testimony last time you were here, this is at T7843: "As to the 13th, I really can't say for sure. I can't remember where I was, probably I was in my office preparing documents for the next day because there were a lot of documents to send these recruits the next day on the 14th." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Because I had a regular instruction or a call-up for -- to serve my -- the -- the service, the regular term. And we had prepared the documents. And I escorted the recruits to the assembly point in Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll get to that. That's the 14th. That's the next day. We'll get to that. Now these men on the buses, the few that you could see and hear, they were prisoners, weren't they? Not people from Potocari who had stopped for the night.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please believe me that I don't know that. At that point in time, I thought these were people who had been in Potocari and who couldn't be bused in the course of the day to the territory under Muslim control and that they were waiting for the day break to take them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Potocari's -- there'll be -- there's testimony from other witnesses, that's about 4 kilometres away. The Trial Chamber has been there. It's about a five-minute drive from Bratunac to the centre of Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's about 5 kilometres away. So, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So would it make sense to take people from Potocari - and my position is these were prisoners, not women and children or anybody else from Potocari - drive them 5 kilometres and then stop for the night and keep them on the bus. If these were all people from Potocari who could go anywhere of their own free will, why wouldn't you just take them back to their homes in Srebrenica and let them spend the night there instead of on a bus on a street?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't ask me. I really don't know anything about that. I told you that at the time that's what I thought. Now whether that's how it was, I really I couldn't tell, nor can I say anything about it now because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. So as you sit here now, you don't know whether there were prisoners held in Bratunac on the night of the 13th of July, 1995? That's your truthful, honest testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say again, I don't know whether these people were prisoners or those people from Potocari. At the time, I thought they were the people from Potocari. Now whether they were prisoners or people who just wanted to be transferred further on, I really at that point in time I didn't think of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So then I assume that from your office in the municipality building, since there were thousands of people on buses who weren't prisoners who were just being transported of their own free will, you probably saw hundreds of them getting off the buses and trucks, walking around to stretch their legs, going to the Hotel Fontana for a drink, something to eat, since they were just welcome people in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's cynical. I really don't think that's how it is, nor was it like that. I just know that there was no military presence in Bratunac at the time. There were elderly people, women and children, and the people on the buses -- the people that I saw, people on the buses, they were guarded by one person, whether soldier a military policeman I can't say for certain. But had they so wished, they could have gotten off the bus and just overwhelmed that one -- all of them together, that one single soldier. That's how I saw it. They were just sitting quietly and peacefully on their seats. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I'm not going to bring it up, but D02262 is a Defence statement of a military policeman from Bratunac named Mile Janjic, and in paragraph 4 he talks about how he was securing buses in Bratunac that night. So, first of all, these people were not free to leave. And, second of all, there were soldiers in Bratunac to guard these prisoners, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the municipal building, I saw, and as I've already said, there would be one person securing these buses, and I suppose this was the escort who would escort these people to their final destination, wherever they were going. That all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me reading you something else from your testimony. You were not aware, this is at T7844 again, that there were prisoner, Muslim men held that night in the Vuk Karadzic school or the hangar, correct? You didn't know that, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the elementary school building? No, I didn't go there. I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Try to answer my question with a yes or a no when you can. Let me read out your answer from your testimony in Blagojevic: "No. No, I wasn't aware of that. Of course, later on there were stories going around but a lot later." So it wasn't until a lot later that you found out that any Muslim men had been held -- or heard stories, rather, that Muslim men had been held in the hangar and the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard later on that there were -- that there had been prisoners there. Perhaps a few days later. It was impossible to conceal that. Whoever was interested and whoever passed by the school probably could see it. I didn't go there and I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, our case is that there were Muslims held in the Vuk Karadzic school, the hangar behind that school, and the stadium, all of which are just down the street less than a five-minute walk from your office in the municipality building where you were. And the Trial Chamber has been there and done that walk. You agree with me it was that distance away?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said in your testimony --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you said that that night in your municipality building less than five minutes away from these sites, you didn't hear any shots. Didn't hear any gun-fire that night?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. Perhaps there was shooting, but I can't confirm. I can't tell you where the shooting was coming from or anything. Well, if I was in my office, I probably -- I didn't hear it, for sure. It is possible that there was shooting. And I'm not saying that the shooting came from those facilities that you mentioned here. Maybe people were shooting in the town itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, let me ask you this: Is it normal when you're working in a municipality building on paperwork getting ready, you know, getting your documents ready for the next day's work to hear automatic weapon fire from less than five minutes away? Wouldn't that be alarming?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would certainly be confusing had it been peacetime. However, it was war time, and nothing was really surprising. If you heard shooting, you wouldn't know who was shooting or why they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your testimony that you thought this could be combat in Bratunac in the centre of town and that that would not be alarming?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not what I'm claiming. I'm not saying it would have had to be combat. People opened fire for no reason at all in our parts. I'm not saying -- it is known that there were prisoners of war there, but I'm saying that I did not see them and I did not hear that someone was shooting. I didn't hear anyone shooting at the prisoners, specifically. I wasn't there. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, as somebody born in Bratunac, who has lived in Bratunac, and was in Bratunac in 1992, and knows that Bratunac had a sad history of bringing Muslim prisoners to the Vuk Karadzic school to the stadium and murdering them there, were you not kind of concerned hearing automatic weapon fire when there are busloads of Muslims in your town again, that perhaps a second layer of blood is going into the floorboards of the Vuk Karadzic school lying on top of the 1992 layer of blood?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question quite well. I apologise. Perhaps you could repeat it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll make it --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. I did live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Since you know the Muslims were killed in 1992 in the Vuk Karadzic school and in the stadium, and you've got Muslims all over Bratunac again in 1995, and you're hearing automatic weapons fire, weren't you concerned as a responsible member of the Ministry of Defence that there might be more murders going on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, that was not my thinking. I didn't know that there was any killing. I didn't know anything about any killing. Had I known, I certainly would have been concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on. You called these critical days. There were busloads, and you've seen some of them, in front of your municipality building of Muslims, you said that they could have overpowered the guard. We've heard in this trial and the view of people in Bratunac that the Muslims of Srebrenica were dangerous, the 28th Division, and it's certainly true that Muslim units left Srebrenica and committed crimes. You also said there were no soldiers in the town. Now you're present, you were 41 years old. You had a uniform. Are you sure that you didn't go and help guard the prisoners, which would be the responsible thing for every man in Bratunac who was able-bodied at that time with all the soldiers gone and most of the police gone. Is it more important to do paperwork than to protect your town?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this interpretation could not -- cannot be understood by anyone. There is something wrong with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask it again very simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why would you not be guarding prisoners since there were no soldiers and not many policemen and it's a critical day for Bratunac with all these Muslims in town?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the chief of the Department of the Ministry of Defence. I was a civilian. I was not military personnel. That's number one. I had specific tasks. I could not deal with guarding buses and prisoner of war, as you say. In those days, I had a task. My task was, as I told you, to prepare the conscription papers and to send recruits to their military -- tour of duty, military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say that were no soldiers after the fall of Srebrenica -- may I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, because if -- it's up to the Court, but you've answered my question and I don't have that much time. Unless you're continue to explain, I understand your answer is that you had your job which was not to guard prisoners so you wouldn't do it, no matter what the conditions in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't my job to guard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. But part of the job, and we talked about it yesterday, of civilian protection is cleaning up the terrain. Ljupko Ilic was in the same building as you, and you knew the next morning, didn't you, that bodies were found all over the town: at the stadium, at the playground, inside and outside the Vuk Karadzic school, in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that Ljupko Ilic worked in the same building and that he was the one who informed me. I heard it from him personally that several bodies had been found in the elementary school, Vuk Karadzic. But as for the town itself or the playground, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac testified here. He's an independent journalist from Belgrade. He was travelling with Ljubisa Borovcanin, who I'm sure you know. He spent the night, Pirocanac, on the 13th of July in Bratunac, and he saw - this is his testimony at T18817 of P00376, "a truckload of Muslim corpses in the centre of town." So a visiting journalist who doesn't even live there was able to know more about the number of corpses than you and civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I was not in the civilian protection. Now, number two, where Zoran Pirocanac was and where he saw that, I don't know. I'm not denying that there were crimes. The whole world knows it, but I never saw the crimes being committed or having been committed, except when I passed through Kravica when I went there with the recruits, passing through. And also in 1992. But you never asked me about that, where I saw some dead bodies in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll get to that. But then just to move on, I think we can move to a new topic then. You agree with me that you know and the whole world knows that on the 13th of July 1995 there were crimes committed against Muslim prisoners in Bratunac. That's what you just said; right? Then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I didn't say I knew back then what was going on. I said nowadays the whole world knows what happened. But it wasn't until quite some time after the 13th or the 14th that I found out we were talking about a crime of massive proportions. What I saw, I saw and on the 14th, at Kravica, dead bodies lying outside the building there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? The transcript has a lot of omissions. Page 10, line 1, he said: "I didn't believe at the time that there had been any killings." And not: "I didn't know that there had been any killings." And again page 10 -- I'm talking about page 10, line 1 now. And here the witness said: "It wasn't until quite some time after" -- or "long after." He said "long after," not "quite some time after."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. I was going to move on but let's just go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long is long after that you heard about the massive scale of these crimes committed in your town and then later in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. That summer. Later that summer perhaps. But the figures being bandied about these days, over 7.000 people, well, that wasn't until a lot later, months later, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about July 21st, 1995? You knew about a lot of killings then, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of July 199-

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One -- five, okay. 21st of July, 1995. Could you please try and jog my memory because that really doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but by 21st of July, 1995, did you know about massive killings in Bratunac and Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bratunac? No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P04398, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, while that's coming up, you can't -- if you don't read English, you won't be able to read it, but I'll just tell what you it is. This is a British newspaper article from "The Independent" from 21st July, 1995. It's about your town and it's called: "Mass Slaughter in a Bosnian Field Knee Deep in Blood." And very quickly, there's been testimony in this case -- the way this information was obtained is that an American journalist parked -- he couldn't get into Bratunac so he parked in Serbia across -- on -- in Ljubovija, across Ljubovija iron bridge towards Bratunac, and he talked to women who were crossing into Serbia to do their shopping. And what he learned and published on the 21st of July was that Serbian women, both residents of Serbia and Bratunac, came across and told him through an interpreter that they were murdering Muslims in Bratunac. One of them said her brother-in-law told her that he and his friends are quite open about what is going on the women said. They are killing Muslim soldiers. One of the women described the main execution site as a playground in Bratunac and said it was terrible. These women said the places were people being killed - this is on page 2 of the English, please - were a playground, also described as a stadium, and at a school, that's the Vuk Karadzic school right by your office, and some kind of warehouse, probably the hangar behind your school or the warehouse, and a dump truck full of corpses being parked near Bratunac. So -- and that testimony -- that -- those articles have been corroborated by our witnesses. So it's your testimony that housewives from Serbia and house wives from Bratunac knew more than you did about the killings in Bratunac in July?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These housewives claim they knew. Who knows if they knew? I didn't know myself, and I can't claim that I knew if in fact I didn't know. These massive crimes, the 21st of July, nor did I see that happening nor do I actually remember that anything like that happened in Bratunac. I don't remember anything like that, and I can be certain about one thing: I witnessed no such thing. There may have been the odd dead body, but the unit in charge of sanitation was probably picking those up and taking them away as they went along. But I can't say that I witnessed something that I factually did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't say you witnessed it. I said this is a small town. Everyone knew what was going on. I'll move on. The 14th of July, this is the next morning, you're driving your recruits to Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is around noon in the morning; right? Or a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Between 10.00 and 12.00. But I'm not sure. Normally we'd be setting out at about 10.00 but we may have set out about 11.00 that day, but that was general time of day, departure from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, and you see -- this is in your statement, you see a huge number of corpses at the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the warehouse. Not in the warehouse. Outside the warehouse. I never left the bus in order to go into the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I said at the warehouse. I didn't mean you went in. Now Jovan Nikolic is testifying either later today or tomorrow, and he was present, he will he say, at the Kravica warehouse on the 14th while the executions were going on. And that was about 11.00 a.m. So you drive by a scene either of an execution or immediately afterwards; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never directly witnessed an execution. When I happened upon that spot, I realised that there was quite a crowd. Many soldiers milling about and the bus was moving at a very slow pace, halting along the way. There is the perimeter wall of the co-op building and there were very many bodies lying there. When I think back, I realise that it was a huge shock to me and particularly to those young men who were with me, aged no more than 18. I figure there must have been at least between 200 and 300 bodies lying there piled about a metre and a half high. At first I thought it was firewood stacked up against the wall when I first cast a glance in that direction, and then I realised what it was. So it really left a horrible impression upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And there were a lot of soldiers there too, you said. You said there were so many that it was hard to drive through? That's in paragraph 40 of your statement. Soldiers in different uniforms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Different uniforms for the most part. Military, camouflage. I couldn't tell the insignia. The last time I testified in the Blagojevic case, I clearly said although I hail from Bratunac and my job requires a certain knowledge of people and military files, at least a thousand --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you -- yeah, you're going to say that you didn't recognise anybody from Bratunac there; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Save you some time. Giving everybody in Bratunac an alibi. Now, you're driving past these soldiers. You're going slowly so you can't even go quickly. Why don't you stop, roll down the window, and say, "What the hell is going on here"? Because that wasn't your job either?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my own assignment to hand over those men at the collection centre Zvornik at a given predetermined time. From there they were to be taken to three different locations, some to Bijeljina, some to Banja Luka, Banjaca, Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't afford to be late.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking where those recruits were and I know you didn't want to be late, but then let me just be -- make it clear, make sure I understand: This is about 15 minutes from Bratunac, from your town, there are hundreds of dead bodies lined up, soldiers there, and it's more important for you to get the troops to -- to Zvornik, not be five minutes late, than just stop and figure out who's been murdered and who's committed crime or what's going; right? You're looking at your watch and saying, Oh, no, don't want to be late.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nicholls kindly speak into the other microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not quite. First of all, I was too scared to go out and face all those armed men there. There were so many dead bodies lying around and I was responsible for this group of young men who were with me. When my task in Zvornik was completed I drove back, and at about 2.00 that afternoon I went to the municipality headquarters to tell them what I'd seen. And they said they'd been long informed about that because Jovan Nikolic from the local co-op had told them all about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask one thing? I don't think I would be allowed to make the kind of comment that was made, for example, at page 16. So I'm asking myself is Mr. Nicholls perhaps enjoying some sort of special privilege here? Lines 24 and 25, page 16 specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Do you like me to ask the witness to answer with respect to that comment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just trying to say -- I was cautioned on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there. How many more minutes do you need, Mr. Nicholls, to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe five, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very quickly. Please answer this yes or no. Do you know that in September of 1995 there was a massive operation to move the bodies of the victims from the Kravica warehouse where they'd been buried initially in Glogova to another location?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't until long after that I became aware of this. Much later, we heard about the operation to move the bodies. But I don't know when exactly or, indeed, where the bodies were taken to. Frankly, I prefer to hear no evil and see no evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Let's move on quickly to 1992. In your statement to the RS MUP in 2005 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 24748. If I could have it up, please. While it's coming up, do you remember giving a statement on the 26th of December, 2005, at the Bijeljina police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Services Centre from Bijeljina inspector was the person who took my interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. So you remember this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember giving a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And you were cautioned and you agreed to tell the truth in this statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of the English, page 2 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can't see it on the top of the page, but from page 2 it started that sentence: "The commander was a certain Peki, the group consisted of 10 to 15 men but later grew bigger." That's about the Vukovar group. But you stated: "I think that there aim was to scare the Muslim population and to pressure them to leave which they partially succeeded in because later they rounded up, maltreated, and killed Muslims, so at that time a major exodus of Muslims from Bratunac took place." And then you say, after the killing of Zoran Zekic: "Following this, as far as I know, Miroslav Deronjic, the then Bratunac SO Crisis Staff president, led armed men to the village of Glogova for that attack." So these Muslims did not leave voluntarily or of their on free will. There was a major exodus because they were pressured and because they were scared; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in that statement at the time still holds true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've only got a very limited time. Now if we could have your 2003 statement up. That's 65 ter 24747. It's another statement of yours to the MUP. If we could look at page 3 of the English. Also page 3 of the Serbian. You state: "The municipal authorities, the Crisis Staff opposed such conduct on the part of paramilitary groups and decided to expel the group from the municipality, and from what I heard the decision was transmitted to the police" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly read slowly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- "... to the police station and for the police to implement it. However, because new paramilitary groups kept coming in, the police was not strong enough to implement the decision. I also don't know who organised protest meetings by citizens against implementing the decision. A large protest rally was held in the centre of town. Citizens protested over the adopted decision to expel paramilitary groups, and I remember that they shouted slogans along the lines of: 'Are you going to expel our liberators?'" And your brother testified about this yesterday. He said: "Well, the authorities were never quite receptive of the paramilitary units," and described how the authorities thought they should be expelled. "However, these paramilitary units had support of the population, so these people rallied outside the municipal building and did not allow -- or rather expressed their support for the paramilitary units." So the paramilitary units took part in expelling the Muslim population that was supported by the local Serb people of Bratunac and it was a factor in the police and the authorities not expelling these units, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we -- may we have a reference? Where were the people in favour of expelling the Muslims? All the people were in favour of is not being expelled themselves. So the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is, I think, an unfair comment to my question. It's very clear from his brother's statement yesterday and this that when the -- that the Muslims were expelling and forcing the -- the paramilitaries were killing the Muslims and forcing them to leave out of fear and that there was a big demonstration in Bratunac in favour of not taking action against the paramilitaries. So my question was fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you repeat your question, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These paramilitary units took part in forcing the Muslim population to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paramilitary units in those days were taking people in, taking in Muslims and killing them. There had already been too much of that going on at the hangar. Many people were locked up in the elementary school gym as well where they were tortured, beaten up, and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the dead bodies were taken to the hangar. If I may just complete this, please. And people were well and truly sick of all this. They could no longer go on watching it or indeed putting up with it. The Crisis Staff, concerned by what was going on, one night took the decision to simply expel them. And also that units of the JNA which at the time was a regular military force, joined by the Territorial Defence, would be the only remaining armed structures dealing with military and defence-related issues. However, the police, being gradually outnumbered by the paramilitaries at the time, was in no position to stand up to them. On top of that, quite a large number of women, particularly grieving mothers, the mothers of Serbs who were killed because mass expulsions of the Serb population had begun also. The burning of Serbian villages. And they took to the street to speak up in favour of their liberators, as they said. That's how they defined the paramilitaries. So that there simply wasn't enough determination to eventually drive them out. That is my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could ask one more question, which is a yes or no question: And the JNA units that were there were of the regular army and the TO units that were there and the MUP never got together as one force to expel the paramilitaries; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like a really big thing when you put it like that: The JNA units. But what you had in Bratunac was a minor military unit, a squad, numbering no more than ten military policemen. A couple of APCs were crewed. So you can't say that these were really strong forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to say something about the transcript again. Page 22, line 25. The witness said "there simply wasn't enough determination." The witness said "there wasn't enough strength." "Determination" is completely wrong and misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you're done, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have several questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tesic, could you help us with this: These people who were assembled there in protest, what were they in favour of? What did they want? Because we're being told here that they were in favour of the expulsion of Muslims. But why were they actually there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason that the crowd had assembled was to try and achieve a certain level of safety by making sure the paramilitaries stuck around. The women there viewed them as experienced fighters who had been involved in war elsewhere, like Croatia, and they saw them as their liberators, or something like that. In Bratunac, we didn't have any experienced fighters or units. We did not have any organised forces, so that was the general drift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about the people assembled there? What were they clammering for? Did they support the continuing expulsion of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. The people were there not clammering for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase. Did they assemble there in order to make sure Muslims were expelled?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did the women assemble there in order to make sure an expulsion was carried out? No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. What was the relationship between the authorities and the Vukovar group? And was it any different from the way they treated any other paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the Vukovar group arrived, they tried to reign by terror, which I -- I did personally experience. They grabbed hold of all of the vital facilities there, such as the bridge to Serbia, the petrol station, to make sure they had sufficient fuel, the municipality building. They attacked some police officers as well. There were more and more of them and they started looting. Large groups numbering 20, 30, and 50 men started coming in, sometimes groups up to 200 men. The few good cars left in the area were also looted and taken. The people of Bratunac took a long time to understand that it was time they took up their rifles and fought for their cause, that they had to fight their own war because nobody else would fight their war for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today at page 16 you were asked about some soldiers that you saw along the road when you were on your way to the recruitment point in Zvornik. Where exactly were those soldiers? Standing along the road or actually in the co-op compound, in the yard, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were soldiers along the road outside the co-op, by the roadside all the way to Konjevic Polje. There were fewer and fewer of them as you neared Konjevic Polje but there were still some soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked today about your role. So tell us if the chief of the recruitment office is part of the civilian authorities or the military structure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we are part of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever met Robert Block, the journalist?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read "The Independent" regularly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the military command or the military administration at any point in time take over control over Bratunac; and if so, when was that? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean military administration?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, how does this arise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, if I may answer. It arises from the question what was done against the paramilitaries in order to introduce law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or it may be related to his role or overall role in Bratunac. Let -- let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that military rule was introduced. The JNA was still the regular army. I remember at the entrance to the municipality administration building, on the right side wall there was a poster, an advert about the introduction of military rule, and the Drina Operational Group was mentioned as a signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Colonel Prstojevic and Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Urosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that they were in the command of the Bratunac Brigade at a certain period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 4719, please. Could we have that on the screen. Let us enlarge the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what induced the authorities and the command to impose military rule on Bratunac on the 30th of December, 1992? What was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, not clear to me why would he need to read the document to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how do you expect me to answer? If you want me to answer without reading, then do repeat the question, please. I remember very well what the situation was like in late 1992. It was very bad. It was only worse after Christmas, once Kravica had fallen and the Serbian forces had great losses. There was much suffering in the Drina valley and the Drina area. Even I, at some time after the 20th of December, although I was a chief of the recruitment office, had to go to the trenches because Bratunac was on the verge of falling. All the entire town was surrounded. They were only 3 kilometres away from the town itself. It could have fallen in a matter of days. So from the aspect of military security, the situation was dire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, sorry, how does this arise from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I was about to ask that. It seems to go -- go too far. How is it related or does it arise from Mr. Nicholls's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, Mr. Nicholls and the OTP, as a whole, seem to assume that there was peace and that the authorities were not willing to do their work. I want to depict the context, what the situation was like, and show whether the authorities could function as opposed to being willing or unwilling to function. When you introduce military rule, then it means that it's a minute before 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put that question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like, and what made the military command and the authorities to introduce military rule.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the field was such that it was a logical move. These were the -- the death throws. We were -- there was a shortage of manpower. There was desertion. There were logistical shortcomings. Everything had to be raised to the highest level for us to be able to defend the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It doesn't arise. This is about Mr. Karadzic ordering military rule on 29 December 1992 which is the witness is saying because of a military threat to Bratunac by the ABiH forces, which has nothing to do with the situation in April/May 1992 within Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a reason that you should have a re-cross-examination. But why don't we let the accused continue his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But haven't I answered already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can simplify were the civilian authorities able to introduce law and order in Bratunac without military rule?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously not. Because, otherwise, they wouldn't have followed -- or wouldn't have issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of this document, what is your knowledge of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I like to put it like this. Only cats and dogs would stroll about Bratunac at the time. Whoever was able to carry a rifle was on the line. It was difficult to provide food for the fighters. Many people had been killed already, especially on the 14th of December, and the situation was growing ever more complex. Roads had been cut off. We had to be extremely serious about the situation in Bratunac. Considering the general military context, we had to focus on the situation in Bratunac because the civilian and military authorities were unable to provide adequate and safe living conditions for the population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here's my last question, Mr. Tesic. There was some confusion about whether you were a member of a civil protection or the TO or whether you were actually an organisational unit of the ministry. As far as you know, did the structure of the TO of Bratunac include any illegal or paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at 65 ter 00744. Do you remember this document of the Crisis Staff dated 13 April 1992? And can you tell us, based on item II, what the TO of the municipality comprises. What is considered a legal military formation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order to form TO headquarters commands and units issued by the Bratunac Crisis Staff. As far as I can tell, this is Miroslav Deronjic's signature, but it looks a bit fishy. The TO of the Serbian municipality comprises the municipal headquarters with headquarters support units and a ODTO, a company formation. What could that be? And then local commune units and the logistical bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How are these units manned, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're manned by military conscripts based on their military obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Military conscripts from where?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Bratunac municipality, those who were registered in the -- with the recruitment office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see in the preamble the following: "Based on the decision on the declaration of a state of emergency in the municipality." Who proclaimed the state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The state of emergency was proclaimed since this decision of the Crisis Staff was issued, because they are referring to it which means that the state of emergency had been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us about the relation of this order with -- with the Law on All People's Defence. Is it -- does it comply with the law, or is there anything wrong?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- don't pretend to have great legal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can help you. Under whose remit was the TO of a municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all municipalities had their municipal TO staffs, and they are hierarchically subordinated to the -- to the higher-ranking staffs and the republic staff, and they were established based on the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thanks a lot, Mr. Tesic. Thanks for coming to testify. I have no further questions. And I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'd like to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tesic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is Dr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pasalic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you to briefly state your full name, your father's name, and when and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: My name is Stevo Pasalic. My father's name was Radivoje. I was born in 1951 at Vozuca in Bosnia-Hercegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your curriculum vitae is part of this report. The Trial Chamber may decide it as a separate document, though. But at any rate, we don't have to go into details. Please tell the Trial Chamber for the sake of the public a few words about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: After finishing primary school, I graduated from secondary teacher training school. Then the teacher training college at Slavonski Brod. And, after that, the Faculty of Mathematics in Novi Sad. Then I also graduated from post-graduate studies in Belgrade, and I obtained a doctoral title at the Faculty of Science at Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't think that your last sentence was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Should I repeat -- should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. And please let me remind you that we should speak slowly and pause between question and answer long enough for the interpretation that you can see on the screen stops. You mentioned the narrow profiles in your education. What was your specialisation? What did you specialise in, in your education?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my education there are also specialised profiles, and mine is demography and social geography which falls in the scope of subjects studied at the Faculty of Science.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please remind us of what we already have in your CV. How many scientific papers or professional papers you published overall?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Our scientific work is evaluated based on books published, papers published, then professional papers that were published, or by participation in professional projects, or by acting as mentors for doctoral candidates. I authored 12 books, which is a lot for a professor, two-thirds of which were from -- were in the area of demography and the rest in social geography or dealt with interaction between tourism and population. My scientific works were published and fall into two categories: Those of national significance and those of international significance. Those that are most highly valued are -- were the ones published on the SCI list. I also presented papers at international conferences or national conferences. There are dozens of such papers. I can't list them all. I also was the leader of about a dozen national -- scientific projects, most of which dealt with applied demography in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also authored many works about the application of the subject matter at schools or other works that were contracted for a specific purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What academic position did you reach? And are you in any academic for -- or do you hold any academic title now?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a well-known fact that professors have to climb up a defined ladder. I started as assistant lecturer and then I became a senior lecturer. After that, associate professor, and now a full professor. And I cover a specialised area which is demography and social geography. This title is permanent and you're appointed for life. I was also invited to become a member of the Academy of Sciences of the RS, or also other organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, could you repeat your last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was invited to other institutions such as the Agency for the Development of Higher Education of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part -- as member of the board, and I'm also member of the senate of the university in east Sarajevo. This is my second term in office there. And I was also elected to the Committee of Demography and Statistics of the Academy of Sciences of the RS. These are my other titles or positions, apart from my position as full professor at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever commended or decorated for your professional achievements?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was awarded several times in my academic career, but the -- I got these awards only for scientific and educational work, which are the two main lines in higher education in line with the Bologna Declaration. The last award I received was in 2012 for my contribution to science, culture, and sport, and I was decorated by the Njegos Medal of the First Order which is awarded by the president of the Republika Srpska. This is one of the highest decorations for scientific work. There are also decorations for other achievements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't recorded what kind of decoration you received.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: It was the Njegos Medal of the First Order. There is also a second order and third order Njegos medal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell me two things: What is your direct insight in the war time events; and where were you during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and grew up there. I worked there, lived there, and I spent the whole war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. My only task during the war was to collect data about any demographic changes and processes in the area I had access to, of course, because in Bosnia-Herzegovina you couldn't move about freely during the war. I collected very valuable experiences that I can present here today. These were empirical scientific investigations or, rather, research, which went on for 20 years. This is extremely significant. Unless you were directly involved in such field-work, this is something you cannot acquire through any other means of education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last question before the break, please tell us about your forensic experiences. Did you ever testify before any courts; if, so, which courts and in which cases?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I can say that I was involved both directly and indirectly. I was involved in the most direct way before this Tribunal in May 2011 in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, when my demographic expert report was fully admitted by the Trial Chamber, which I consider a great success in my scientific work. Likewise, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when it comes to demographic research that had to do with the war time events, my -- the results of my work have been or will be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I note the time. Perhaps you have already decided about the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour. We will resume at 4 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic, would you please tell the Trial Chamber what you were asked to do by the Defence in this case -- or for the purposes of this case.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of this case, I tried to show in a very complex way the demographic movements in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, before the war, and also the effects after the war. But before that, I analysed in detail and provided a critical analysis on the expert opinions of primarily the -- the expert Ewa Tabeau, and then I researched in detail the sources and the methodological process which are the two cornerstones for any expert report of this nature. Then I presented my own findings that I arrived at by using a completely different scientific method and methodological process, whereby I wanted to show that there are other approaches in scientific research and investigation so that we can see whether the results would be the same or whether they would differ, which, for me, is very important in this work of mine. And, finally, but not least important, I wanted to show with my report this complex picture of -- that had changed as a result of the war but that would have changed even absent the war, which is an interesting approach because you follow events that are caused or the result of war developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for instance, but you also want to see what would happen if there was no such war, so you simply try to observe all of this and then compare it with all available data. So, in brief, this would be the outcome of my research and this is what the Defence primarily wanted to -- wanted me to present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By separating phenomena that would have happened even if there had been no war and isolating phenomena that happened as a result of the war, what you did accomplish in this way?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: It is very significance when preparing a complex research paper, especially in demography, to be well acquainted with a tendency of a phenomenon in a case like this. So even before the war time events, during the war, and after the war, you need to look at how this phenomenon continues after the war, and then you can come to a more complete picture and factual information, and then would you get a more precise historical picture. If you were not to proceed in this way, you would get erroneous statistics and a false historical picture, and that would not be satisfactory for the needs of any scientific research. Now, what have I done in this case? I prepared a retrospective of demographic developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1948 - which was the first census after World War II - up until 1991, which was the last census taken in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and today 20 years later there is still no new census. And I observed the tendency of the movements of the population which were quite marked even in peacetime, even at the time when Bosnia and Herzegovina was -- had the highest rate of development in the economy and science and cultural. Now toward the end -- what did we observe? Toward the end of the war, Bosnia and Herzegovina completely changed the character of its population. Before the war, it had entered the so-called transition period, like all the other developing countries in the world, which was the result primarily of the birth rate and the deaths of the population. The birth rate was falling and dropping, where now in Bosnia and Herzegovina the birth rate was the highest in the former Yugoslavia since 1948 on -- and onwards, and then there was this complete change, and I can prove this. I can show data here that there was a fall in the birth rate and in 1991, overall for Bosnia and Herzegovina, it can be considered relatively high. However, it is more significant to observe it as a differentiated natality or rate of birth, because then you can see that the natural birth rate was 14 mils, so to translate: 14 children would be born in 1.000 people of the Muslim population --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could the witness please step back and repeat his last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, could you repeat from the part you referred to 14 mils.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Not 14 millions. These are relative data that are expressed in vital statistics in mils, which means a thousandth portion of something. In other words, the Muslim population in 1991 had the birth rate of 14 children per 1.000 inhabitants in the Muslim population. So we say 14 mils and that's what it means. Now the Serb population had the -- the birth rate was twice as small, so it was 7 mils; 7 children in 1.000 of the population; and the Croat was 8 mils. Now, I want to stress that this information is very important when we look at the structure of the population by age, and I believe that we will get to that later during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does this affect the strata of the combat-ready population or the able-bodied population in relation to the participation of the underage members of the population, and how does that differ among the different groups, the Muslims, Croats, and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: What noticed is that the Prosecutor, the OTP experts did not deal with these variables although they are significant. There is one population - the Muslim population - that has a very high birth rate of -- so there is a large participation of the youth population, meaning under the age of 18, whereas this picture is quite different for the Serbs and the Croats. So this gives a completely different picture within the structures of these populations which will have an affect also in the war time conditions, including in some civilian jobs areas. I could not say perhaps with detail what that -- how that reflected in the background in terms of the military use and on the front line, but this data is a variable that significantly affects the overall presentation of the population at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell the Trial Chamber what was the percentage of minors in the Muslim, Serb, and Croat ethnic group, respectively?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Basically we all use apocryphal figures. There's no one in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including OTP experts, who would have explicit data about this. But if we draw an analogy to this information, the percentage or the representation of the minors is far greater in the Muslim population as opposed to the Serb or Croat populations. That, of course, also depended on the local authorities and the way that they recruited minors, even minors 17 or 16 years of age that were recruited by the Muslim authorities at the time. But, in any case, there is a far greater proportion of those in the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us how this would reflect or whether this would have an effect on the estimation of the losses of the able-bodied population and why is it important, in other words, to establish what the percentage of able-bodied men or population there is in each of these ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: That is a very significant question. I noticed that the OTP experts, when they made this differentiation between combat -- combatants and non-combatants, they did not use this qualification or -- which is more interesting. They did not have data for the entire population. So how can you make a differentiation? How can you distinguish civilians from soldiers if you're not -- if you don't have information on the entire population? So this is quite absurd for the purposes of certain studies. They used information that was secondary or tertiary and quite unreliable. So there is a great difference and various information were used from research to research, and you could even say that it's amateurish when doing this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go back to the -- to the tendencies that you observed. What did you observe, what were the natural tendencies in Bosnia and Herzegovina or trends in the population movements in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: There is a rule that says in order to know the present, you have to know the past very well and have a vision of the future. Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the ethnodemographic sense, is a very complex area. If we look at the history, it is the most complex demographic area in the former Yugoslavia, and whoever wishes to obtain valid research and valid results must know the historical makeup or the historical character. The people of Bosnia and Herzegovina were a historic part of that country. Now the largest per cent of the Serb population tended to leave for Croatia and migrate to Serbia. The Croat population migrated to Croatia, whereas the Muslim population tended to remain in place or perhaps migrate to Sandzak or Turkey or some other areas. As a result, in the late 1980s, Bosnia and Herzegovina lost annually through immigration 15- to 17.000 people; in other words, they left that part of the country. This was on an annual basis, which means that in a period of ten years, that is up to 200.000 people. Now, bearing in mind that these were the vital category of the population, usually between 20 and 40 years of age, in other words this is a reproductive category, a fertile category that could still produce off spring, that was very significant. Now these were the trends before the war, even -- now had it -- had the war not happened, these trends would have continued to a certain degree. Because the war broke out, they were only generated further and they were somewhat intensified. Let's put it that way. And the proof of that is that when we look at the end of the war, we see that the trend of leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina continues, and if everything is summarised, in the 20 years from 1991 to 2011, Bosnia and Herzegovina lost 90.000 [as interpreted] people, not as victims of war but through the loss of the birth rate and the migrations, and, of course, indirect victims of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "15- to 17.000," is that the ratio between immigration and migrations or is it just the people who were leaving or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I will answer your question, but I notice that there is an error in the interpretation. It's not 90.000. It is 900.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Now talking about the migration losses, this is what we would call the migration ratio which is obviously negative. In other words, those who came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, minus those who left, the result is 15- to 17.000 less people coming than going. But Bosnia tended to be a -- tended to be the part of the country of the former Yugoslavia where people tend -- more people tended to leave than come to reside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any information as to where the population that came to Bosnia and Herzegovina - that immigrated into Bosnia and Herzegovina - where did they settle and what ethnic background were they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: It is well known that the trend is primarily the Bosniak population, because there was a higher rate of their arrival into Bosnia and Herzegovina as opposed to their leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina, as opposed to the Serb population. Now as for the distribution, these -- this population mostly settled in urban areas or close to large rivers where the density of the population was the highest, whereas the traditional Serb population was, for the main part, distributed in the mountainous areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Should we then assume or conclude that the demographic ratio would depend on the ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Most certainly. It most certainly would. And we can here invoke our primary sources, the most primary sources available. Ever since the 1970s, last century, what was then the Muslim population and the Bosniak population started becoming the dominant population group in Bosnia for reasons of migration but also because of the increasing birth-rates. At the same time, the Serbian ethnic group in particular and the Croatian ethnic group were leaving more and more for Serbia and Croatia respectively, thereby suffering losses in terms of the demographic share. Both in relative ratio and the absolute ratio, their numbers, in terms of the overall share, ethnic share in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were on the wane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. People moving in and settling, the Muslim immigrants settling in cities, specifically, and towns, how did that affect distribution of the population in terms of urban and rural factors? Who predominated in the cities and towns and who predominated in the rural areas?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: It's very simple phenomenon after World War II. In the bigger cities and towns the Muslim population tended to be predominant, Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Bihac, and so on and so forth. The Serbs predominated in terms of numbers in Banja Luka alone of the major cities and the Croats only in Mostar. But if you look at how these cities and towns and their populations evolved, this is a trend of constant expansion. That applies throughout the world and also in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So predominantly the population of the larger cities and towns was Muslim. Traditionally and historically the Serbs tended to settle in mountainous areas. That is part of their tradition and that is how they held on to their property also, because the Serbs tended to own such property in these areas that was then handed down from generation to generation which created strong links to these areas that were not urban areas. It's still obvious 15 to 16 years after the war, the Muslims tend to focus on the cities and towns unlike the other two group, particularly the Serb group which tends to be in small villages or in entirely rural areas. These are historical processes. There's nothing subjective about them. It's all about facts, incontrovertible facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that before the war ever happened there were certain trends in terms of people coming into the country and people leaving the country and the general ratio was negative at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. What about the trends before the war, specifically in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what exactly went on?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, as I pointed out already, the demographic trends were not suddenly triggered by something at the beginning of the war. These trends go back a long way in history but became particularly prominent, carrying to the fore, in other words, in the latter half of the 20th century when the whole world began to explode in demographic terms. So in relation to the number of inhabitants in 1941, the increase by 1991 was 71 per cent. The overall population. In Macedonia, we had the only figure that actually exceeded the BH figure. That was 76 per cent increase. So these were large-scale sudden changes and the population moves about internally. So these internal migrations definitely affected the distribution in terms of specific regions and areas within the country. Even before the war you had the Sarajevo-Zenica lowlands, predominantly Muslim, and then the Bihac region or the Tuzla region. The -- the lowlands in the north-east of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the low lying areas. You also had the Serb population which tended to remain in the north-east. Mixed population in Central Bosnia for the most part, Muslims and Serbs combining in that particular area, although the Serbs constituted a minority there were also some Croats in those areas as well. Eastern Bosnia for the most part mixed population, Serbs and Muslims in this case, with a purely symbolic number of Croats living there as well. So this was the process that was in progress at the time. We call it the ethnic and territorial homogenisation. It's a technical term. My research proves that the process is ongoing to this very day, and if you look at the population groups shifting in terms of internal migration from one area of the country to another, it just goes to show that the process is still in progress, the ethnic and territorial homogenisation.
