Sarajevo has over 90 per cent Bosniaks today; Mostar is divided into the Muslim half and the Croatian half; Banja Luka predominantly Serb, so is Bijeljina; Zenica is predominantly Muslim; Tuzla also predominantly Muslim; and so on and so forth. So that is the process that we refer to as the ethnic and territorial homogenisation which is not yet completed. It still goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we forget about the war for the moment. Can you try and tell us what this phenomenon looked like before the war. Was the trend perceived and who went where in terms of internal migrations within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: As I've pointed out already, if we forget about the war for a moment, there are certain ethnic areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout one of the three groups was predominant. It is a generally known fact that eastern Herzegovina is predominantly Croat. If -- if anything, the figures had been boosted by more Croats coming into the area making their ethnic predominance even grater. If you look at the large important river valley, the Sarajevo-Zenica valley, the Gorazde area also, the Bihac-Krajina area, or some other areas in Central Bosnia all are all predominantly Muslim. Had it not been for the war, they would have held onto these areas, obviously, in terms of ethnic predominance. The Serb ethnic areas are more extensive but not as densely populated we might say because the absolute numbers in terms of overall population were smaller in relation to the Muslims. So that is the area that we normally refer to as the Krajina with Banja Luka at its centre. And then you have Eastern Bosnia, the Semberija area, parts of the Drina river valley - eastern Hercegovina in particular - traditionally the population there is predominantly Serb. As for Central Bosnia, this area tended to have more of a mix in terms of the population there, the Muslims always being the predominating group. I am trying to put together some sort of retrospective for you in terms of the trends before the war, and then try to imagine a situation in which the war did not happen at all. What exactly would have happened? I wish we had an ethnic map in front of us so that I could point it out for you and that we could all follow visually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Had it not been for the war, would there have been more mingling between the various groups or do you think the ethnic and territorial homogenisation would have gone on unhindered?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If you look at the factors of history, there are a lot of important factors in a complex area such as Bosnia-Hercegovina. These all point to one fact: Incontrovertibly, the homogenisation process would have gone on unhindered and the ethnically pure areas would have further solidified, which does not mean that relations between the groups would necessarily have deteriorated. But we're talking about a type of traditionalism here. So that is why I'm adamant one must know the history of this region in order to be able to monitor these trends all way up to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now ask you to please explain the importance of information sources and the nature of information. The sources that you used or in a comparative sense the sources used by OTP experts. Can you tell us about any similarities or differences that you found in terms of relevance?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: This is one of the most important issues brought up in our reports, the expert report of the OTP, on the one hand, and our own on the other. As I said a while ago, when we talk about reports of this nature there are two cornerstones: The sources on the one hand and the methodology on the other. The sources, the methodology. You have the OTP on the one hand and you have us on the other. There are differences between the two. So it was particularly interesting to see whose information would look more valid. What do I mean when I say information sources? There are so-called primary sources. The most relevant sources, the most valid sources. In as far as you have any access to those, those are the first that you must invoke. You get your information from a primary source. Just by way of an example, a good example of a primary source would be the census, although many objections can be made to the way the census was conducted in BH in 1991, or, indeed, to any use of the 1991 census as the primary source of information, which we state clearly in our report. We even went as far as the quotes of the expert reports previously produced by the OTP. That information was then processed or indeed published following the 1991 census. Yet in our reports, we were able to get this information but not before 1998. Therefore, we decided to use the reports. But that is a huge shortcoming for the OTP expert report because they failed to use a principal primarily source of information like that at all. They used imaginary forms and calculations which will hardly give you the real picture of the situation. OTP experts for the most part found themselves using secondary information sources. What type of information can you derive from that? You can use that type of information as a supplement, as something to supplement your primary information, simply because the relevance is not there. Secondary information was not generated by official authorised institutions such as the statistics bureau or some state bodies. We can specify exactly what is involved in that type of work in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but here is an example: The 1997/1998 census lists. And then two key sources of information for the OTP, the 1991 census, and the 1997/1998 list. They use what is called a matching or cross-referencing method which yields a sea of figures but fails to deliver a realistic portrait of what actually went on in the area. Unlike the OTP reports, the one that we drew up ourselves, we took a totally different approach. We tried to go and seek out other primary sources of information. So the most authoritative institutions will produce these sources, and the most authoritative individuals, researchers looking into the question. I'm talking about the census, of course. I used those sources. I picked out a number of variables and opted for a totally different method in terms of how I went about calculating the information and the phenomena which was in stark contrast to the approach taken by the OTP expert. Necessarily, the results diverged. The one advantage of our report is we used primary information sources. These are available and I'm in a position to present some of them here today. I would like to have an opportunity, if I'm allowed one, to use some examples to show how this type of information is calculated in relation to single municipalities, and this is information that is actually used in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are doing an excellent job simplifying these complex matters so that we might be better able to understand what you are saying. But can you tell us how certain variables can be measured if you use the census as your information or the list as the control group and the experimental group would be, for example, the list? You have the census on the one hand and the list on the other. So if you cross-reference the two, what do we end up with?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I think we're talking about two widely diverging principals here. The census is the most comprehensive survey that you could possibly have in a given area. Regardless of any shortcomings of the 1991 BH census, we have to invoke it as a relevant source for our purposes. On the other hand, a checklist is something that might be used for the purposes of cross-referencing or drawing far-reaching conclusions about the phenomenon at stake. In this case, you need to use the list, the voters' list. And then you quote OTP sources saying the lists were voluntary, so that's what they say. People were free to register as voters and perhaps not. There were several locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina where you were free to go and vote or perhaps you have no desire to vote at all. That made no difference. In our opinion it was the 1996 list that actually has more relevance, because that was right after the end of the war. But we never quite got that far. So the matching methods, if you look at the very complex aggregate picture, constitute an attempt to qualify a certain phenomenon. You have the 1991 census and you're trying to see how they faired according to the 1997/1998 lists or electoral roles. This is simple enough but you also run the risk of neglecting a lot of other complex facts, population movements, migrations. But what drove them? Was this a situation where they had no choice? Was this something that they did of their own free will for families to be reunited or what have you? Why did someone decide to leave, for example, an urban area and move to a rural area or vice versa? Was it for professional reasons? But this is something that expert reports never reflect. This is a thorough deep going scientific analysis, and that is something that is obviously lacking in any of the OTP reports. When we talk with statistics - it ask not my intention to offend anyone - statistics can be used to prove just about anything. You can toy around with the figures, but without an in-depth analysis you can't arrive at real reliable results. So that's the one thing I wanted to say about the method used in figure matching. We decided to change tack and apply different methods. So if you have the age structure of the population and you look at that, why would I come up with a totally fictitious sample if I actually have real information, good information from 1998 released by the federal statistics bureau of Bosnia-Herzegovina called the Annual Journal for Statistics giving you accurate figures on the 1998 population structure for the first time after the war? So the age structure according to categories is very clear-cut. You take that as one variable. You take the natural trends as another. And if you look at vital statistics it's always available for you to use. You can also use fertility, the fertility of the female population as a useful indicator. So, in other words, use a whole different methodology. You apply scientific methods and you obtain a final result which can be defined as a scientific conclusion, and this is very different from the results obtained by the OTP report. So that was the objective of my work. I wanted to turn things around and show that if you use different methods, even simpler methods in this case, you can arrive at totally different results and what actually happened throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us try and see in which ways demographic changes came about, especially when it comes to demographic losses. And you may be able to show us what affected these, especially in the work of the OTP experts, which factors were taken into consideration in assessing the causes of demographic loss? Do we have a knowledge about population in third countries or in neighbouring municipalities? Can these be considered losses? And what have you -- what do you have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Of course. In the past 20 years, my scientific interest was also in demographic loss in Bosnia and Herzegovina without anticipating such an event as the war. We, as demographic experts, are also obliged to deal with this issue. The question you asked me is extremely complex and nobody can tell you how high the demographic losses are, including direct demographic losses due to the war but not limited to that. The Judges certainly know that two relevant sources were used for that. The Mirsad -- Mirsad Tokaca's CID and the reports of Ewa Tabeau of the OTP. The losses are estimated at 97.000 in Tokaca's version, 204.000 in Tabeau's version. But these are only the direct losses caused by the war. These are not the overall demographic losses. When you calculate those, then you must look at them in war time conditions and in peacetime conditions. What would have happened in a country? This was my approach and the direct losses caused by the war do not differ much. I made a calculation and, of course, these figures are approximations. Nobody has direct insight into the reality and nobody will even say they have because it would sound frivolous. And according to my estimates the directly losses amount to about 110.000. These losses are the most painful but they are not the only ones. They are pure demographic losses both due to the war and also those that would have happened if there had [as interpreted] been a war. Those are losses due to lower birth rates because a certain number of children was not born because there was a war. But the greatest losses are migrational demographic losses. They were very high before the war as well, and I explained that. During the war, migrations were generated about 2 million people moved within BH or went -- or crossed the border, left it, and then you can follow this process further. After the war there is a more intensive return to Bosnia and Herzegovina that amounts to about 500.000 people, but a great number stay in other countries and even apply for citizenship. Based on my calculations, my estimate that from -- from after the war of 1996 up to now, 120.000 people left Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if you take all this into consideration, you come up with a total of 645.000 people which is the total of migrational loss, which is huge for such a small country. But the OTP expert did not take that into consideration, and it is very difficult to look at something in a isolated fashion. And then we come up with what I have said already, in the past 20 years Bosnia-Herzegovina lost 900.000 people. If BH would have had 4.7 million people if the census had been made earlier, now, the country has 4.377 million people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the expert please slow down and repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, interpreters couldn't catch you after you said the country has 4.377 million people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I repeat: Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1991, according to the census, had 4.377 million people. These are rounded numbers. If there had been no war, under different demographic conditions, the estimate is that in 2011, it would have 4.7 million people, which was interpreted. And now what was not interpreted: This shows that such a small country lost a total of 900.000 people, in inverted commas. Directly and indirectly. And the conclusion is that today's estimates of the official statistical organisations, that is the BH statistical agency, is that Bosnia-Herzegovina now has 3.83 million people, which is about 900.000 less than there would have been under different conditions of demographic development. I'm referring to the time-period ending in 2011.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 50, line 8, of the transcript, Dr. Pasalic did not say "without anticipating the war" but "without anticipating this trial." He worked without anticipating these trials here. And then line 15, Dr. Tabeau did not say 402.000 but 104.000 -- expert and -- and 732.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Out of these 900.000, how high would the figure be without the war assuming that the negative trend of 17.000 would have accumulated in 20 years? How many would there have been with the war or without the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: It would have been interesting to follow the demographic development. I tried to show that BH entered demographic transition before the war, which means its population was changing. The population is aging. There are fewer children born and people live longer, which happens in developed countries. In 1991, the average age of the BH population was 33 years. Today, the average age, according to our estimates, is about 40 years. And this trend would have continued even without the war. Let us compare other countries, surrounding conditions: Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, they are the same demographic trends. Their -- the average age of the populations of these countries is over 40 years. And let me tell you, for the first time in history, in 2007, Bosnia-Herzegovina has a process of depopulation. Fewer people are born than are dying. That had never happened before in the demographic development of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These changes would have been inevitable even without the war. The war only generated or accelerated some processes. First of all, the distribution of population. But these traits would not have changed even without the war. But this is a world-wide process. If we look at the global population, we'll see what the dynamics are in -- overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your confirmation that there would have been 340.000 even without the war did not enter the transcript. So please repeat. If this negative demographic trend of 17.000 per year, how much would the -- how high would the aggregate number be after 20 years with the war or without the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, that's very -- that's a simple calculation. That means 20 years times 17.000, which amounts to some 250.000 migrational losses. But there's another component, pure demographic losses; namely, a lower birth rate which sank both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in other countries. And if we take that into consideration, we would come up to a total of 340.000 overall demographic loss. Let me conclude. Even in -- at most peaceful times, Bosnia-Herzegovina's demographic development would not have been what it was like from the Second World War until the 1990s. And there are the same trends that can be observed in surrounding countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this is a matter of criminal law, please show us to what extent can we make reliable conclusions about the illegal nature of the -- the migrations of population within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers, I would object. I would object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't believe this witness is here to speculate about the illegal nature of migration and I also think the question is vague as well in terms of what it's asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you would like to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I think if Dr. Karadzic specifies what he means by "illegal," I think that would clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with Mr. File. Could you clarify what you meant by "illegal"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expelling too; that is, driving people out. Ethnic cleansing. The allegations of the OTP imply that the losses are the result of illegal expulsions of population. And I'm asking Dr. Pasalic what conclusion can be drawn from this information and from both the OTP report and his own report about the legal quality of these processes during the war, taking into consideration that there were such trends even before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. If you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be brief. It is very bold and it's a simplification to draw such conclusions as can be found in the OTP report. There are allegations that these are unnatural trends and so on. I tried to show that the problem is much more complex and that it is really very bold to make such conclusions. I would not dare draw such conclusions which, to my mind, are biased and do not reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you proceed, can you take a look at OTP report where such conclusions were drawn? Mr. File, do you agree that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm -- I was asking whether you agree that OTP expert drew such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Oh, no. Not at all. I believe that Dr. Tabeau's report makes no commentary on the motivations but it's a statistical report, so I would also be interested to know where in the report he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Karadzic, separate from this issue, you are coming to some concrete numbers. You -- you -- you will show us some concrete examples. Hearing in the abstract, it's very difficult to follow in concrete terms. Yes, Doctor, do you have it with you? Or, Mr. Karadzic, you can show us that part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, Dr. Tabeau was not invited to a scientific conference but to prove that I was responsible for demographic changes. She was not even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Dr. Pasalic said OTP expert drew conclusions which is very bold and he would not dare draw such conclusions which are biased and do not reflect something. So I wanted to see the conclusions of Dr. Tabeau, which she drew in her report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break, I will be able to reply to this, Your Excellency. But the very nature of Dr. Tabeau's evidence was to show that I'm responsible for demographic changes in order to corroborate the allegation of the OTP that these were a result of a forcible displacement and persecution of the non-Serb population. So it's very clear what her task was. And, after the break, if you still expect me to, I can provide more information where this is implied, if not explicitly stated, that the changes are as a result of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was asking the doctor. Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a misconception. Dr. Tabeau's evidence shows what the demographic changes were, and there are thousands of pages of transcript and thousands of exhibits that show what the motivation for those demographic changes were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask then, if that is so, why then did we exclude the movements and migrations of Serbs from the report? Because the nature of relative numbers requires that both variables be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not follow your submissions. Your point is that, why you are prohibited from dealing with demographic changes on the part of Serb population. Is it your point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If what the Prosecutor has said is correct, that Dr. Tabeau only showed without prejudice the movements where people moved from, this cannot be seen either in absolute on relative numbers unless we also take into account the migrations of the Serb population, and even more so when we talk about relative numbers and percentages because they are interdependent. And so I ask myself, if that is so, how and why is Dr. Tabeau's report going to be used as proof of my guilt, and why was she called to testify here if we are not, in fact, prosecuting here for guilt for -- for war crimes? And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I will not delve in debate further. Yes, Doctor, did you take a look at Dr. Tabeau's report and found where she drew conclusions to that effect you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first, I would like to tell you that I've looked and studied all the reports of Dr. Tabeau, beginning with the Milosevic case and all the others. And what she has actually used in her study as the -- she used the term "war" in -- "... by figures." I do not have her conclusion in the transcript right here and now, but based on what Dr. Karadzic said, the sentence that he used, and I don't see it before me, I explicitly said that such a conclusion could not stand in the context of all the very complex changes that I spoke about here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to enter in: On page 60, in line 14, I said that these relative numbers are "interdependent" and not "independent." The relative growth of one population is linked to either its inflow or the outflow of another group or population or a combination of the two factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about this, Dr. Pasalic. And I'm referring to paragraph 24 of your report. Could you tell us what you meant by combat battle deaths? And there you actually refer to two authors. Could you tell us what types of deaths in a war, especially in a civil war, can be identified.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to come up with a theoretical definition of this type of death because in various reports, including the OTP expert reports, the approach taken was rather free and loose and there was no use of standardized documents when this issue was investigated, the issue of deaths. Although there are documents from hospital records and so on that could be used. Now I used some theoretical categories that are accepted throughout the world. There are four categories. The battle deaths, then deaths due to increase in one-sided violence, unorganized criminal violence, and non-violent mortality. Mortality in war time is always greater than mortality in peacetime. Why did I stress this? Well, because I did not find this clearly defined and investigated in the expert reports in the -- in the OTP expert reports where they deal with deaths and the number of people who died during the war. Then it was their duty to make this distinction, but I do understand that they couldn't not do it because they simply could not -- they did not have access to raw primary data. These are the so-called standardised documents that are the only valid documents that show or confirm the death of a certain person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, based on your experience, what is the share of each of these categories of deaths in civil wars? Do you have any information to that effect, either from your own investigations or studies or reference materials?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that in some of the reports, not only of the OTP experts but others, there were numerous reports on Bosnia-Herzegovina, this issue was studied or approached rather loosely. There was no differentiation made between combat, combatant, or non-combatant, or civilians, and then there were some biased conclusions that the death was the result of one or another factor, and I did not consider these valid, and I simply insist - although I do not have the primary sources either - but I insist that if we want to be precise, we should make this categorisation because that is how it is done according to international standards. Now, according to my opinion, there were not only battle deaths involved in the war. There was also an increase in mortality as a result of illness and mortality of children and so on. So this -- or for any other reason. So this is what is lacking in all of these expert reports, OTP expert reports on Bosnia-Herzegovina, which then, in fact, undermines the validity of their reports. I do not, unfortunately, have specific information to tell you the data shows this and this and this, but I can't do that because that would not be appropriate for an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that a transversal investigation or research would be useful, could you tell us how a longitudinal research such as you conducted during the war, how that kind of research -- what would its assessment be in terms of accuracy as compared to what your colleagues from the OTP did? Did this research of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the question be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even your question was not interpreted, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your observation of the developments during the war and your research of this phenomenon, did it have -- was it of a nature of a longitudinal research and what is the value of longitudinal research as opposed to transversal research, and especially in view of the secondary sources of information?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Over the past 20 years, I applied longitudinal research as well, and to make it clear, this means to research or follow certain phenomenon in continuity, in succession. So this is what I said at the beginning, that I did research before the war, during the war, and after the war. There's also the transversal approach which is the approach where you observe a phenomenon at the same time in various areas which can be seen in the research -- in my research, especially in a time -- during the war time in various areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Such research always leads to more valid and scientifically sounder outcomes. This is one of the shortcomings of the reports, the expert reports by the OTP experts because they only use data from one period, one certain period; for instance, if you only take 1992, that cannot tell you anything about what was -- what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina over a period of time. So this is why I stress the need to use the longitudinal approach as well as the transversal approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to say that, for the transcript, that the Doctor said the transversal means to -- the transversal approach means to observe a certain phenomena at one point in time in several areas, several different areas, not in one and the same area.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you notice or conclude, rather, and register, applying scientific methods about the migrations of the population after the war and after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: When the war ended, or after the end of the war, you can clearly see in my research that the demographic trends in Bosnia and Herzegovina continued and they were negative. So there was a drop in the birth rate, a natural depopulation, as it were, immigration, in other words, people leaving, and a redistribution of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina which we can see from the statistics published by the bureau of statistics on the internal displacements of populations. We see that there is a larger trend of the population moving towards Republika Srpska and a greater trend of people moving into the area of Brcko. That's -- I -- I see that there is a connection between the two, and, in any case, after the war there is also a number of negative trends in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The population -- the number of population is dropping, the population is growing older, the younger population is smaller, but most probably there will be a stagnation and a great migratory loss because simply there aren't so many immigration countries that could accept people migrating from Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is my general conclusion because there are few immigration countries that easily allow people to migrate into their own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain in table 17 of your report how it came about that Republika Srpska has a positive demographic growth and who are the people returning or moving into Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: In my report, I presented one such datum, and I used of agency for statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 2011, and we also have information for 2012 as I said here, and the trend is the same. You see in Republika Srpska that the number of people who moved in is greater than those who are moving out, and that the -- the -- that trend is positive. Now with immigration, the -- there's a greater number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to catch up with your speed. Could you repeat. And, in the meantime, shall we upload that. It's on English page 68. I do not know the e-court number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, the table -- table number 17 which was produced on the basis of official information from the agency for -- statistics agency, Bureau of Statistics for Bosnia-Herzegovina which provides this kind of information regularly on an annual basis. We can see that Republika Srpska has, in the course of the year, a greater number of people moving in than out, which means that its migration ratio is positive, whereas opposed to the BH federation and the Brcko district where the ratio is negative. Now, this is only based on information from 2011 but the trend was present in earlier statistical data from the time when internal migrations were being monitored. And this is from 2007 up until 2012. I do not have that information but they do exist. So this also shows that there is a continuing redistribution of populations within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, as we said in a statistical sense, there is an ethnic territorial homogenisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one quick question. How could this represent a trend if it is limited to the year of 2011 and to the place of Brcko district, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I said that I only gave an overview of 2012. And you're right, taken alone it wouldn't be correct. But I also added that this has been monitored since 2007, and that throughout that period, from 2007 to 2012, the trend is the same. It is positive, the migration trend is -- or ratio trend is positive for the RS and negative for the federation and Brcko. I'm sorry I don't have the data before me here, but this is something that I have observed and, I repeat, it repeats and is continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic, can you tell us what is the share or what is the affect of war time events or interethnic tensions or the Serb authorities on this? To what extents are the Serbian authorities responsible for this; or, rather, what is it that the Croats and Muslims are fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'll say this: Everyone whoever wished returned to Republika Srpska and recovered their property because that is a personal choice. So I will mention several areas where large numbers of Muslims returned; for instance, in Zvornik, 25.000 Muslims returned to Moslem after the war, or Kozarac near Prijedor and that entire municipality. Other hand, and this is very striking, is the fact that Serbs are not going back to the federation, not even those who traditionally would want to return to their own land, to their hearths, as it were, because that has not been provided for. The buildings have not been reconstructed and there is also no way of providing for the livelihood. There -- economically speaking there is no livelihood. Now, in the former -- in the former territory of the federation there were 17 per cent of Serbs in the past, whereas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request: Could the witness repeat the percentages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you -- could you start again from the part where you referred to percentages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said, in answer to the questions why Serbs and Croats are leaving the federation still, even 15 years after the war, I said that according to some estimates, or according to the estimates of the Bureau of Statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are only 3 per cent of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina federation today. There are 75.5 per cent of Bosniaks, 25 percent of Croats, and the rest are the others. Now in 1991, there were 17 per cent of Serbs within the same borders of the federation that are today. It is estimated that there about 400.000 Croats in the federation today, whereas in 1991 there were 750.000. So I will repeat what I said before, that Serbs and Croats are gravitating towards Serbia or Croatia respectively. On the other hand, I will repeat, the returns to Republika Srpska have practically been finalised, and, for instance, in the Zvornik municipality, 25.000 Bosniaks returned to their land and their homes. This is information from -- based on Bosniak institutions -- information, information produced by Bosniak institution -- information, information produced by Bosniak institutions because they keep records on -- on this, and they're especially careful about records where reconstruction and recovery of private property is concerned. So this is the difference in the migrations that we showed in -- an explanation for it, that we showed in table 17 or, rather, why is that the -- that the growth is positive in Republika Srpska and negative in the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us, what is your basis for the conclusion that you should focus on 20 municipalities in the federation or 65 municipalities in Republika Srpska? Could you tell us how representative is this sample? What is its nature? The interpretation is a disaster. I will try to be simpler for the interpretation. Of the total number of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was around 148, as opposed to a total of 62 new municipalities in Republika Srpska, to what extent was the sample of the 20 municipalities that were scheduled in my last indictment, to what extent is that representative for drawing conclusions on phenomena in a systematic way?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If I want -- if I were to be explicit, I can say that it is absolutely not representative. Not only when taking these 20 municipalities, but also when other samples are taken into account because they used the so-called appropriate or suitable sample, so that when you base a sample according to some kind of a position that you want to take, you will then get an erroneous statistic or statistical data and historical picture, which means that that information is practically not useable, especially so when it has to do with such complex cases as is this one. What would have happened had we taken only the 62 municipalities of Republika Srpska, or the same number of municipalities in the Federation? That would give us skewed data so it would not be representative in any way. Without seeing or taking an overview of the entire area, you will not get a true historic picture and the correct statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I see what time it is and I am expecting your intervention. And if I can just say that Mr. Ram, thanks to Mr. Ram's kindness, we've just learned that today we have reached the 365th day of this trial, which means that we have been sitting in this courtroom for a full year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he also told me that next witness will be 300th witness in total, including the Prosecution's witnesses. Well, given the time, we will take the break for 45 minutes and resume at 18 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we include Mr. Momcilo Mandic, who was a Chamber witness, Dr. Pasalic is the third -- 300th witness. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic, you told us something about the representativeness of the sample to do with the 200-something or perhaps 62 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. How do you see the category of others in the findings of the OTP's expert witness? What can you tell us about that? How did the witness treat that group, Serbs, Muslims, on the one hand, and others?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I would say that a degree of confusion arose in the treatment of this particular group, others. Why? We have the 1991 census in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to that census, there were some subjective reports indicating there about 100 ethnic groups and nationalities there. Serb, Croats, Muslims, the three constituent peoples, and as many as 97 other categories, ethnic affiliations, some more numerous and some very few. According to these reports, they're all classed as "others." And what I find to be particularly indicative, a category of those people who at that time declared themselves to be Yugoslavs who accounted for the greatest share in that category by far. I think that is the particularly liberal interpretation if you decide to class the Yugoslavs as belonging to the category others. In our own reports we analyse that in far greater detail, demonstrating that the category of Yugoslavs traditionally was linked to the Serb population and to a far lower degree the Croats and Bosniaks which is simple enough to demonstrate. You take a town such as Siroki Brijeg in western Herzegovina. We have 1 or 2 per cent Yugoslavs. And then you go to a place like Banja Luka, predominantly a Serbian population, and the share of Yugoslavs suddenly rises to between 15 and 20 per cent. So it was particularly significant issue, how that category, the Yugoslavs, would be classed and viewed in the reports. I think it is definitely an oversimplification to class them as others. When I covered Sarajevo and other regions, I decided to take a different approach. I used relevant estimates in accordance with such indicators as were available. So the issue remains open. What about these others, because that is a category that is continually referenced in OTP reports which then changes to a significant degree, has a significant bearing on the indicators regarding everybody else which then distorts the historical image and the actual truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I then summarise by asking this: Is there perhaps another aspect which leads to a distortion of these historical image. So it's too narrow a sample. The first thing. The second thing, the discrepancy in terms of the number of minor persons. And then the third thing is this category which is defined as others. How does that affect the relative indicators of loss or sufferings of the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, in relation to these three categories? So what -- in what way does that affect the result?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: According to my calculations, that affects the realistic representation, depiction of the actual situation. You have relative indicators which is something that is very much taken up by the OTP experts because for the most part they did not have absolute figures available to them. I wanted to link that up to a particular data point which I quote in my report. If I may, what is this liberal interpretation based on information sources or indeed based on the categories of ethnic affiliations that we have been discussing? There is one thing that I can demonstrate here and I think that would actually be desirable here in court, for a document to be scanned that I have brought along. We have Ewa Tabeau's statement, you have my statement, you have Smajo Cekic's statement who is the director of the war crimes institute in Sarajevo, and you have Dr. Muhamed Sestanovic who was in charge of a project -- the census project in Sarajevo between 1992 and 1994. You will see that there is no such list, no such census, no such information was ever published, yet Ewa Tabeau in her report invokes just that information which is quite arbitrary because it's been 22 years since the war and we still don't have a proper census. Who could have drawn up such a list during -- in the very thick of the war between 1992 and 1994? That would not have been possible. You have all these statements collated of all these people who are actually involved. I have the photographs too accompanying those documents. So we could make a scan of that just to show how work proceeded in a most arbitrary manner in no way proving the representativeness of a process or a particular event. Or if we just take this single piece of information, the funerary company belonging to one ethnic group and then trying to represent the numbers of persons from that ethnic group who were killed or died in Sarajevo throughout that period. I deem that to be entirely unacceptable and you can't base a report on that because the information becomes irrelevant. If you are adamant about using a source which simply does not exist, then 20 years later it still doesn't exist. The information of that alleged census was never published. They try to justify that by saying they had problems with their technical equipment, technology, the software, and so on and so forth, but how could the data ever have been produce to begin with? So from a purely scientific viewpoint this is entirely intolerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about during the war? How many Croats or Serbs could possibly have been buried by this funerary company, the Bakija Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, unless that was necessary, such burials were not performed for Serbs or for Croats. Each group had its own company that was in charge of burials and they looked after that kind of thing. That's why I'm greatly surprised to see serious researchers accepting this as their sole source of information or for the purposes of cross-referencing in order to arrive at the overall number of victims during a war in such a large city. They can't possibly use the data generated by a single company as a reference. This is sheer nonsense. That's how I would define this from a scientific and research viewpoint. We simply wouldn't use anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also put forward an opinion saying that the -- a reduction in the number of variables or markers broadens your choice. So if you take the first name and the last name, that sort of broadens the scope, and if you take the father's name, that sort of narrows the scope. So what ramifications stems from that treatment of variables? And what is the overview obtained, if, for example, you want to get the -- you want to base your findings on a set of ten markers or categories?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If you take that approach, the greater the number of variables the better. In present day circumstances when we have all these data points available to us, we use as many as 15 for purposes of our research. That, however, is not strictly necessary. If you bear in mind the conditions at the time, the more variables were available to us the more reliable the information thus retrieved. If you just used the first and last names that is not sufficiently reliable. It is better to use other information in case it's available to you, the identification numbers of the person involved, the parents, the gender, the -- the date of birth and so on and so forth. If you take all these variables, the result obtained will be more reliable regarding a whole population group or a section of a particular population group and that's why we are adamant that these variables must be used yet they weren't used by OTP experts, and they were in a position to use them because as early as 1998 such information would have been available to them. And Ewa Tabeau started her report back in 2000, two years after all this particularly relevant information was made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In your report you also include your own research regarding Srebrenica. Could you briefly tell us what your conclusions were and what method you used to arrive at that conclusion in relation to the OTP reports and your own research?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about my personal approach and also about researchers, generally speaking. Srebrenica is a particularly complex issue which must be approached with caution. We have to err on the side of caution and not be too liberal in the way we deal with our information, so we tried to arrive at a demographic conclusion concerning what occurred in that particular area. My conclusions for the most part say the following: In order to draw up reliable demographic analysis on missing persons in Srebrenica, whether dead or missing, first and foremost you would have needed valid statistical documents available to you produced on the basis of reliable information, which is the most vulnerable point of any report on Srebrenica that we have seen so far. There are all sorts of liberal interpretations and treatment of data by various associations and as a rule large scale discrepancies occur between all of these. In many cases, the sources are not reliable and sometimes people simply don't have a sufficient familiarity with acceptable scientific methods or statistical methods which leads to considerable confusion when conclusions are drawn on the relevance of such statistical indicators as are actually used in these reports. You see what they're using in these reports: ICRC lists, Medecins Sans Frontieres lists, census-related information, the electoral role from 1998, a data base on displaced persons from 2000, information regarding exhumations and bodies that were actually identified. What am I trying to say here? What am I trying to underline? If you look at all these information sources with the exception of the 1991 census, none of these sources are susceptible to any known and legitimate statistical standard which results in an incredible number of mistakes. It is impermissible, the mean value being 30 per cent. And that would be our conclusion regarding the demographic conclusions derived based on this information. The possibility is very much open from our perspective for anyone to seriously come to grips with the issue, because now there is more information available and more valid reliable information available that could be used for that purpose. May I just name an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, by all means go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I quote a specific example there, not as a whole in my report but it's in one of my attachments. If you use the cross-referencing method as it was used by Ewa Tabeau in 1991, she denotes a presence in Srebrenica, and then in 1998 she's talking about the electoral role. We contact some institutions who deal with gathering such information and then we receive a list containing the names of 3.500 persons on the role back in 1998 yet are missing from the 1991 census in which they were indeed not registered as inhabitants of Srebrenica. So this is an impressive number which suggests something about the demographic trends in the area. That is a glaring example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to know about the representativeness of the stratum. One question. What about the age category of those aged 90 or over 90 years of age? Would the death rates in that particular category be taken as representative in relation to the overall population? How would that work?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: From a demographic standpoint, when we talk about mortality and any figures that might be taken to be representative, we need to arrive at a standardised mortality rate of the overall population which you then use to process reliable information, and you also need to consider differentiated mortality rates because it's not the same for those aged over 90 who are nearing the end of their natural lives or indeed for people who are between, say, 20 and 40 years of age. This is a delicate issue. When you talk about mortality in war time or indeed in peacetime, one must distinguish between these categories, and you need to apply what we call the standardisation method to ascertain realistic mortality rates of the population in certain circumstances. So if you look at people aged over 90 can in no way be taken as representative of anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Much along the same lines, what can you tell us about the representativeness of certain age groups of the male population in relation to their ability to fight or their involvement in fighting? What are the results obtained if you look just at that category, which is not representative but, rather, is limited in terms of the year of birth?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at just one group, one category, a limited sector of the population, according to their age group, you derive a picture which perhaps does not reflect the phenomenon in its entirety, although it is a generally known fact that the male population - generally known, I'm saying globally known. Some of the categories are reduced because of the men that were killed in war so that obviously affects the overall figures for the male population. Needless to say, the global tendency is 106 men are born for every 100 women, so more men are born than women on a global scale. And then from age 14, age 15, the female population sort of takes over, and there are quite a number of factors contributing to that change. Among other things, war is something that needs to be taken into account, but then also males are more susceptible to certain types of illness, or perhaps performing hard physical labour which can also lead to greater mortality rates among the men. So just to bring that as a point, you can't simplify these matters when you look at these reports. Mortality is a delicate issue even in war time circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about men's hazardous lives, smoking, gambling, drinking, an unhealthy lifestyle, how do you think that might affect the mortality for men as opposed to the mortality figures in relation to women? Do you think that has a bearing on that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. The average life expectancy on a global scale is greater for women than it is for men. In Bosnia-Herzegovina which is what we are looking at here, right now, life expectancy for women is about 75, for men it is about 72. Even without the war. So that addresses the issue you have raised, and it also tell us about a number of other factors that affect the shorter life-span of the male population. Back where we come from, the life expectancy is still more shorter than you might expect it to be in developed countries, highly developed countries, Japan, western Europe, and so on and so forth. The conditions of living is, obviously, is one thing that really affects this trend. And the male population where we come from is easily tempted by all these risks, the risks of an unhealthy lifestyle, smoking, drinking, gambling, and so on and so forth. So this is something that you must take into account when you talk about male mortality in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 107 of your report you quote one sentence from the OTP report's expert, the author. I quote: "There's no proof that a significant number of persons who disappeared when Srebrenica fell have survived." What can you tell us about the validity of this conclusion? From the forensic point of view.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't think your -- the page numbering is the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's page 108 in the English. It's the first paragraph, first complete paragraph of page 108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Footnote 49.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I enlarged the font size so the page numbers have changed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found the footnote. There's no evidence that any significant number of the Srebrenica-related missing persons have survived. This is the quotation and the footnote reads: "Report on the number of missing and dead from Srebrenica of 12th February 2000." And then the page references. What I wanted to show with this quotation is that this is a very general statement. Nobody was trying to prove whether anybody survived or didn't survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pasalic. I have no further questions at this point. I also want to leave some time to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, if you are still interested in what I said about the implications of the findings of Dr. Tabeau, I can quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First, we shall admit Doctor's CV. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection to admitting Dr. Pasalic's report, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Not an objection, Your Honour, but just one observation which was that I noticed on page 111 in the English at footnote 60 it refers to a list of persons featuring on the 1997/1998 voters' register list but not in the 1991 population census is given in a separate annex to this report. And I haven't seen a separate annex to the report. I think the witness also referred to this as attachments today around transcript page 77, although I don't believe it was recorded in the transcript. But I just wanted to make that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably can you take -- take it up in your cross-examination. Yes, we'll admit the expert report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3125, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. File. I take it your cross-examination will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could leave five minutes at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: One of your primary critiques of Dr. Tabeau's municipality report, which is P4994, is that it is only based on statistics and it does not investigate the individual causes of the migration that took place between 1991 and 1997. I noticed at paragraph 66 of your report, you complain about the use of dry figures, and at paragraph 67, you say: "Our main objection is that the demographic trends and other developments in BH in 1992 to 1995 were much more complex and go beyond the mere drawing of evidence and conclusions on basis of numbers only." Now if you were doing a scientific study to identify the reasons that individuals moved at a particular moment in time, you'd conduct a survey with individual interviews; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: This tool, such as a survey or questionnaire, can be used to research this phenomenon, but you can also use other tools. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, today at page 35 and 36 of the transcript, you described how you collected data during the war in the area that you had access to. Now that was data that you collected with individual interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Correct yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And that was interviews of exclusively the Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Basically, yes. Because, unfortunately, there was a war and our movements were limited. It was impossible to collect data in an area to which you have no access. Neither was it possible for others to remove -- to do research in areas accessible to me, nor could I go and research in areas that I couldn't physically go to. But I conducted empirical research by means of surveys --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Right. Okay, Professor, I understand. My question was just whether you had access exclusively to the Serb population, and I think you answered that question at the beginning. You didn't put any details of this in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I think that I made a comment in my report and said although this report reflects mostly my research among the Serbian population, it can give a significant contribution to the creation of an overall picture of all demographic processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, taking into account other reports or the work of other researchers if they are scientifically acceptable. Two years ago the Trial Chamber accepted such a report fully, although it only dealt with the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your report there are no details of what methodology you used or any copies of surveys or forms or questionnaires that you gave to conduct this research. There's no indication of where to go to review these materials. There's no indication of what territorial boundaries applied to your research. None of that is in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I could give you a simplified answer, but let me take you back to the period when this data was collected. It was war time and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: To be honest, Professor, I would be interested in a simplified answer.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: A simplified answer is I collected the data on behalf of the State Centre for the -- for the research into war crimes and all the data are -- can then be found in the archives of that institution, such as individual questionnaires and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Right. But --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: -- whereas I presented the synthesized results in three books that have been published.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Again, that wasn't my question. My question was: You didn't put any of that in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: That would have required a report that is thousands of pages long. If I were to include individual questionnaires and so on. That is inappropriate. But you -- instead, in such a report, you include references to the sources where these findings can be checked and corroborated, but nobody has yet disproved the accuracy of the data in my report. Nobody from scientific circles, and that is very significant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment on the transcript. The reply of Professor Pasalic from line 18 on is not accurately reflected. The synthesised results of the research have been published in three scientific books. None of that was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is partially there. Let continue. Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now you mentioned during your direct examination that you wrote a report in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case and that you testified as a witness in that case. I want to ask you about some of your testimony. On the 12th of May, 2011, at transcript 20636 in that case, you said: "I was in an area where I could study demographic processes involving the Serb population. After the war, after a certain amount of time, the conditions became right for such research as well. However, Ms. Tabeau's research, as well as that of the IDC from Sarajevo, had already been rather all encompassing, so I believe that anything I would have done would have been duplication. I thought that all of this put together would have provided a more realistic and more comprehensive picture. That is where I see the significance of my own research, although it did not include all the demographic processes because that was impossible. Finally, I did not have the capacity to do that, to study a span of ten years. This is a lot of work and to this day practically no one succeeded in doing that." Now, to clarify, to the extent that this case is concerned with the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from the indictment municipalities, your research does not add any data regarding reasons for population movement of Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Let me answer the question like this. Yes, the quotations are the very ones. I was replying to the Trial Chamber that I mostly dealt with the sufferings of the Serbian population and that after the war there was no need to conduct research into the Muslim and Croatian populations because it -- that had been covered in many other reports, but the -- but data for the Serbian population was missing. That was the significance of my report and that's what I wanted to explain back then. I didn't want to discuss ethnic cleansing because that is a rather complex term which I also tried to explain then before Court. And when a number of researchers compare the results of their research, they can arrive at relevant results. In the past five years, I was the only one to research demographic -- the demographic situation in all of BiH. Nobody has yet disproved my results. Everything was based on scientific sources and nobody ever challenged my results, which, of course, is a source of satisfaction to me as any other researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So, to be clear, your answer to my question is no, your research does not add any data regarding reasons from population movement of Muslims, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I gave examples in that report. I took the municipalities of Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Prijedor as examples. The method of calculation of the numbers of the Muslim and Croatian population were wrongly applied. And this is one of the most explicit ways of challenging -- challenging allegations of what happened in certain municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Maybe we're not -- maybe we're not being understood. The question is about your own research with interviews, not about looking at numbers. The point is you never added any data through interviews of the reasons for population movement of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, I would say that the area was not accessible to me. I could not conduct a survey among the members of other ethnic groups. There was a war and freedom of movement was limited. I had a very clear task which certainly considered the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you about this theory of ethnic territorial homogenisation which you have mentioned frequently today and it permeates the report that you wrote. Now, this is a theory that you developed; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: No, not only I, but I am one of those who developed it. But other demographers and sociologists that deal with the processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina came up with this joint thesis, ethnic territorial homogenisation as a historical process, which was present before the war as well, generated during the war, and continued after it. It is very easy to proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You believe that ethnic groups naturally tend to want to live apart from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: During the period of homogenisation, it means that a certain trait is homogenised. Ethnic affiliation is something that is present in Bosnia-Hercegovina. It is not a product of the war exclusively. The war could have catalyzed it. But what is -- what are these things that are happening after the war? I showed you the internal migrations in Bosnia-Herzegovina nowadays. This is a process of ethnic territorial homogenisation which needn't be seen as anything bad in itself because we're talking about a complex ethnodemographic area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript did not reflect everything that was said. I think that the relevant service should listen to the tapes again and check the transcript against the tapes and not merely correct individual mistakes. I would have to intervene about every single answer. I understand that this is technical and perhaps the interpreters are not familiar with demographic terminology, but something must be done. So these tapes must be listened to -- listened to again and the transcript corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Pasalic, could you speak a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, again, in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, on the 10th of May, 2011, at transcript page 20479 and 20480, you said: "Serbs or Croats are always focused on the neighbouring countries, that is to say, Serbia and Croatia, throughout history. As for the Muslims, or now Bosniaks as they are called, they were focused towards Turkey, so the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina is an immigration area exclusively up until this day." And today you said a comment similar to that at page 42 of the transcript. So did you mean that for the various reasons that you've enumerated such as economic factors and social factors that Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina have always had a preference for moving to Turkey?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I merely wanted to back this up by historical facts, that the Muslims, but to a much smaller extent, were leaving for Turkey, whereas Serbs and Croats traditionally went to Serbia and Croatia respectively. I showed that by mentioning specific figures, most Serbs after the Second World War left for Serbia. Croats for Croatia. And the Muslims were much less susceptible to leaving BiH, ten times less, but when they did leave they mostly went to Turkey or other Muslim countries, which is natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This theory of yours has not been adopted in international academic circles; right? It's -- I think the way you put it in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case was it is not a known thing internationally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It doesn't sound like anything I may have said. But if we were to develop this theory in the scientific circles of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the question is to what extent we would agree about all these movements, but let me not give too long an answer. I know how the intellectuals in Bosnia-Herzegovina see these migrations. Other people see them differently. But this is a fertile ground to develop different theories for migrations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and out of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to show you the transcript page so can you see where you said that in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we switch to Sanction for this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So this was a question to explain the theory. And you said that all your explanations of ethnodemographic movements in the war. "And I also researched the postwar period can corroborate the basic thesis that I put forward and that is the ethnic territorial homogenisation. This is not a known thing internationally." Does that help you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Everything can be of assistance, but I really don't remember saying this. Maybe I forgot. Maybe it was misinterpreted. And international is also a bit vague. It's too loose a term.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, regardless of the validity of the theory, it does not explain on its own why a particular group would move at a particular time; right? You still need some form of information to put population movement in context; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question. But migrational movements out of Bosnia-Herzegovina have been very intensive, and all forecasts say that they will continue to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- I'll clarify. In your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, on the 10th of May, 2011, at transcript 20515 to 516, you said: "This is the principle of territorial ethnic homogenisation of ethnic groups which shows that there was a transfer of population. Sometimes it was caused by ethnic cleansing. Sometimes it was caused by deportations and prosecution." I think you meant persecution. "I've already explained that to you. These processes continue to this day." So my question is: Your theory of ethnic territorial homogenisation does not exclude the phenomena of ethnic cleansing or forcible transfer of populations?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, let me try to recall that report and why I used the categories ethnic cleansing, transfers, and deportations. All of these are internationally recognised forms of movements of populations, and I wanted to show that everything that the OTP experts did was not a deep analysis and practically allowed for all of this to be bundled together as ethnic cleansing which is not correct. Ethnic cleansing is a quick and forceful removal of a population from a certain area and that was not the general phenomenon in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, and that was the context in which I explained this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. That wasn't the question. The question was your theory the territorial ethnic homogenisation doesn't exclude any of those types of population movements. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, if you want an explicit answer, ethnic territorial homogenisation is a process that was happening during the war and also after the war and it can be motivated by different factors and motives. One of them, at the time, was the war and the general insecurity and uncertainty that where the population felt safer in their ethnic area, which -- where they were the dominant ethnic group. But why is that still present today? What are the motives today? Those are the answers that I would like to show because --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: -- to point out how complex the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina were regardless of whether you're satisfied with my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: How about this: When I read to you your testimony where you said sometimes it was caused by ethnic cleansing, sometimes it was caused by deportations and prosecution or persecution, that -- you confirmed that was your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see that? Was it actually said, "caused by" or "referred to as"? So did Dr. Pasalic say, was it "caused by" or was it "referred to"? In our language, these two words sound very similar but the meanings are very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm reading the transcript to him. If he denies it, we can look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for me it's quite clear. We can call something ethnic cleansing. Some processes we can refer to as transfers of populations. Some we can term as deportations or we can use other terms. All I was trying to point out was that the OTP experts did not go deep into these analyses, and, in a way, by presenting their figures, they practically showed that this involved only ethnic cleansing and that is not acceptable. Ethnic cleansing has a definition in -- within the international framework and that is what I abided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at P2639, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you see in front of you is a decision by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most from 4 June 1992. And you see under conclusions it says: "Mirko Vrucinic, Nedeljko Rasula, and Colonel Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. "First category: Politicians. "Second category: Nationalist extremists. "Third category: People unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. "In view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps." Now, does this look to you like the sort of government order that might cause population movement independent of these other factors that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: You are putting to me a document that I didn't have while I was preparing the report in Stanisic/Zupljanin, nor for this case, and I do not feel that it's necessary for me to comment on it at this point.
