This is absolutely the first time that I ever see a report of this kind, these type of conclusions and so on. This has nothing to do with my report and I have no idea where you got it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, it's evidence in this case, and I'm wondering what your view is on it.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you my arbitrary opinion. This was mainly something that was dealt with and agreed at the local level. These were not orders that came from the Supreme Command or the government. And there were also arrangements between municipalities for transfers of population. For instance, in Kozluk 10.000 Muslims were -- they left that area in a peaceful way and saved their lives and then they returned to those areas because it was war time, and for them this was the most acceptable way in which they could be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In the Stanisic and Zupljanin case at transcript 20503, you said: "When, due to the forced migration, a group of people from one ethnic group comes to one specific area, then indirectly pressure is exerted on another ethnic group who had been living there earlier, that ethnic group feels more insecure because war implies many terrible things. People have left their family members, some extremists or paramilitary groups appear, and great insecurity is felt by the civilians, and then people were willing to leave everything they have, all their property, and go to territory which they would consider to be more safe which was most often an area where their ethnic group was predominant. This is what I called voluntary migration." So my question to you is: The sort of migration that takes place under this kind of pressure, to you, is voluntary; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to expound here on migrations, but I remember very well that this statement that I -- that you see here, I corroborated on my own example from the area where I used to live. I left that area, although there was no rifle pointed at me, and went to an area where my ethnic population was dominant and where I felt safe. In this, I tried to show the principle of connected vessels and the movements of the populations right before the war because this started happening before the war broke out because the population wanted to avoid the uncertainty and feel safe in the areas where they were. That was a vital issue in those areas. These were rather spontaneous migrations, you -- that would be the way to put it, rather than expulsions and persecutions that would be accompanied by brutality and so on. But at the same time this does not mean that there weren't any extremists or paramilitary formations that actually acted in quite a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to change the subject slightly and ask you about this issue of declarative ethnicity. You mentioned at transcript page 71 today that you analysed this question in far greater detail. This was relating to the inclusion of Yugoslavs in the category of others. Now, in your report, at paragraph 38, you say that the biggest problem with this is that there was no way for people to declare ethnicity in 1997 when registering to vote. And you also say that over the six years there was a change in declarative ethnicity. This is on page 18 to 19 of the B/C/S version. Page 20 of the English. And then in your report you describe what you say are changes but here I don't -- I don't see any citation or any study or any evidence that supports this claim. Is that correct, it's not in your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understood your question exactly. What is it that you're asking me about and what you want me to answer? Are you asking me about the Yugoslavs which was one of the categories in the censuses up until 1991? No --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm asking you for evidence to support the claim that over the six years there was a change in declarative ethnicity. And I'm wondering where there's any evidence for that in your report.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, the census was conducted the last time in 1991, an official census. And there was the category of Yugoslav as an ethnicity. After that there was not a single census and this is a hypothetical question. Namely, who would declare themselves as what ethnicity. If that's what you meant. Nor is there anyone who can give you any explicit data on how people declared -- chose to declare themselves after that, because this is a subjective choice of any individual person and that's the case everywhere, including in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But if you meant the category of Yugoslavs, it is evident that this category contained a large percentage; in other words, this -- this whole array of ethnic declarations where people declared themselves as Yugoslavs, there were a whole -- there was a whole range of different ethnicities, but they have disappeared. They are non-existent today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's switch to that topic, then. I asked whether there was evidence or a change in declarative ethnicity. You didn't provide me with any indication in your report where you have evidence for that. So I'm going to ask you about your comment at paragraph 40, which is related to what you just said. You said: "It's widely known that when the category of Yugoslavs still existed, it consisted mostly of Serbs who have always favoured the preservation of Yugoslavia and even the creation of a new Yugoslav nation which was much less present in Muslims and practically negligible in Croatia." Now, again, you don't cite anything to support this assertion in your report either, do you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I've tried today in my testimony to point out this category of Yugoslavs where the case was that most Yugoslavs, most people declared themselves as Yugoslavs in those towns where Serbs were in the majority. And, as an example, I talked about the chamber of municipalities and local communes of 1991, where a large -- where a majority of Serb deputies won in those municipalities, although they did not have a majority in the overall population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the last portion of the answer be repeated. This witness was too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, you're again speaking too fast. I take it you read English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat from -- you -- the example you gave about the Chamber -- Yes, you'd like to move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I just -- I don't think that answer was responsive to my question, so I'd like to put a slightly different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's fair enough. But in any event please speak slow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean there was no answer? It was not answerable. Dr. Pasalic said: "I talked about the participation of Yugoslavs in Serb and Muslim areas or towns." What do you mean it was not responsive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was whether he cited anything in the report or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: My follow-up question is: I'm not asking you about speculation based on political developments. I'm asking about scientific studies or any other kind of scientific evidence that supports this assertion.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, no one did any research in this category of Yugoslavs. There was no such -- there is no such research or study in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now doesn't that statement that Yugoslavs are really Serbs, doesn't that violate the basic premise of the census which is that people are free to declare their ethnic affiliations; in other words, despite what people believe, you are going to tell them what they really are. Is that how you're approaching this?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: No, that's not my approach. That is the approach of the population that freely declared their ethnic affiliation in 1991 where some 7 to 8 per cent in Bosnia and Herzegovina declared themselves as Yugoslavs. But then after the war, that category no longer exists in Bosnia. There are four categories: Bosniaks, Croats, Serbs, and others. And, of course, in science circles there is the -- the issue arises as to where those Yugoslavs are. Now, because there was no census, there hasn't been any census, we apply the principal of analogy. According to the territorial distribution of this area, we showed that such categories did not exist in Zenica, Tuzla, Bihac, Sarajevo, which are predominantly Muslim towns. Where the population -- the dominant population was Serbian, it actually inflated their numbers because they were in mixed marriages and Serbs are generally traditionally -- they had traditionally -- traditional emotional ties with the concept of Yugoslavia which they had created several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I think this comes down to a question of methodology. You say in paragraph 40: "The authors should also have calculated the proportion of Serbs in the category of others and then used the result to correct the data from the 1997/1998 list." Now this would be methodologically highly inappropriate would it not, because it would be arbitrarily changing census data?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I've explained that the 1997/1998 information from the voters' registers are irrelevant and they're unreliable for me or any other researcher. This was also something that the OTP experts pointed out. It's -- it's a very arbitrary principle. We could not find any solid data on the basis of which we could find reliable data on what someone's ethnic affiliations is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That wasn't -- that wasn't my question about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That wasn't my question about the source in terms of the voting register. My question was about changing data that was in the census about ethnic affiliation. That would be, you agree, highly inappropriate from a methodological standpoint; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question, how could OTP experts back in 1997 or 1998 by applying that methodology possibly have changed that affiliation and put together others and Yugoslavs? Where did they get the right? It is our belief that the category of Yugoslavs cannot be subsumed under others because that accounts for two-thirds of the others population. It's absurd. It's too much to subsume under that category, a heading, and this is where we part ways with the OTP experts on the issue of Yugoslavs as opposed to others. That's why we're challenging their theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're going to stay with this page of your report. At paragraph 41, you say that: "In table 1 of the addendum," you're referring to P4994, "the authors present calculations performed only for Serbs and the Muslims. The fact that the Croats and others and a considerable number of Serbs among them were excluded from the general population in this sample and that all of the values are expressed in relative number which in turn have been the most affected by the exclusion of the Croats and the others makes this calculation far from realistic." And my question is: Did you actually read table 1 of the addendum? Because I would refer you specifically to table 1C which relates to Croats and table 1O which relates to others and provides statistics for both of these groups on page 32 and page 35 of the report respectively?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember all of the tables for the Muslims, Croats, Serbs, and others. I didn't comment on that in the same context though. Hence, the definition. We calculated the Serbs and Muslims because we used them as reference points from individual municipalities mentioned in this case, where Croats and others were a statistically negligible group simply because there weren't that many of them around.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have to confess I'm a bit puzzled by that response because that's not the way that it's written in your report. You just say that the Croats and others were excluded from the general population in this sample. Doesn't that misrepresent what's in the Tabeau report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: No. In my report, I dealt with the Muslims, the Croats, the Serbs, and everybody else in one of the attachments. Maybe it's the context of the sentence where this is said that leads you to that erroneous conclusion. But my process -- the information on everybody, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and others alike are there. The methodology used is different from that applied by Ewa Tabeau and the results too are different. That is easily demonstrable. But I did not gloss over those additional criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about what was in your report. I was asking you about what you said was in the Tabeau report, but we'll move on. I'd like to move to English page 39 and B/C/S page 37 of your report, which is paragraph 111. Here you're talking about the method of calculation and you say: "Our method of calculation differs from that of the Prosecution experts. We did not use the matching method but rather a selection of various variables to calculate the aggregate indicators for each of the ethnic groups. From several possible variables, we used the variables relevant to the size of the total or a specific contingent of the population and the natural movement (natural population growth rate for each of the ethnic groups)." And then after that you list some variables, and then you produce a table, which is table 3, which has numbers and percentages along with a footnote that says: "Calculated on the basis of a number of variables, specifically taking into account the number of live births, natural population growth rate, differentiated by ... different [sic] ethnic groups, taking into account the different levels of the rates which provides highly reliable data, with mistakes possible within statistical error only." Now I note, again, here there's nothing about your methodology. Reading this, no one could even try to replicate what you've done because you're not revealing how you arrived at these figures; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Not correct. I disclosed my method in terms of how I arrived at these figures in a different figure. We're talking about differentiated birth rates providing different information based on the variables. And it gives a different result as compared to the OTP expert's result in relation to the overall number of persons born up until 1998. Their age of consent falls in 1998. Until 1998, they were under age. My indicators show the ratio between non-Serbs and Serbs, telling us that a greater share of the Serbian population born by 1980 because the Serbs are unrepresented in the up to under 18 years of age category because of the lower birth rate, and this is a very significant factor that is entirely overlooked by Ewa Tabeau in her reports. That is the gist of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Again, I'm --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: And later we'll be coming across specific variables between each and every ethnic group, and that is what I've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about whether you named any variables. I'm asking how you got to these numbers that you put in the table. There's nothing that shows how you made any calculations here. Can you point me to a paragraph where you explain that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'll be glad to. Table 2, age, gender, groups, category; in the B/C/S, it's 37, page 37 of my report. You can find that the variables for age, the groups, overall population, male, female. Source, Annual Gazette for Statistics, 1993 through 1998, Federal Bureau of Statistics. Ewa Tabeau failed to use that source which is unfortunate because it is the most relevant source if we're after variables. And that is where I get my information on the number of inhabitants, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims born by 1980 and then after 1980. This is incontrovertible information and it's not something that I concocted based on nothing. And then have you all the calculations in the table, paragraph by paragraph; 110, when you have the result; 111, which is based on previous calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, let's be specific here. Table 2 says: "B H Population by Age and Sex According to the 1991 Census." There's no break down between Serbs, Muslims, Croats, or others, yet you're telling me that that is the basis for generating table 3 which has a percentage break down by ethnic group of persons born before 1980 in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, again, there's something missing here; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: At first sight, your observation is correct. This is universal data for the overall population of Bosnia-Hercegovina, but then I apply a different variable called differentiated birth rates. I can't specify the paragraph at this point, but you find one for each of the ethnic groups. A certain statistical formula is used in order to carry out this differentiation according to the ethnic group break down and based on the age groups, because in the report you don't have the age groups according to each of the ethnic group clearly distinguished and I had to use my own standards to calculate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. You do the same thing again -- well, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour wished to have five minutes, so I'll pursue the rest of this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll continue tomorrow, Dr. Pasalic. But before we adjourn there are three matters I would like to deal with. The first will -- the Chamber will issue an oral ruling in relation to General Krstic's testimony. On the 7th of February 2013 in light of Radislav Krstic's refusal to testify for medical reasons, the Chamber ordered the Registry to file a more detailed medical report evaluating Mr. Krstic's physical and mental health and to consider whether "testifying in this trial would indeed be detrimental to Mr. Krstic's health, and if so, in what way," and whether he has a basic capacity to understand the questions put to him and give rational and truthful answers to those questions. In accordance with this order, the Chamber received the Deputy Registrar's submission concerning independent medical expert report which was filed confidentially on 8th of March 2013. The Chamber has reviewed the medical report and the answers provided by the examining neuropsychiatrist regarding Mr. Krstic's condition and the extent to which testifying in this case would affect his health and whether he was able to testify as a witness. In light of the answer to question 2 on page 7 of the report, the Chamber does not consider that the concerns raised in the answer to question 1 reach a level that would preclude Mr. Krstic from testifying in this case. In light of this report, the Chamber finds that there are no medical reasons which would amount to good cause for Mr. Krstic not to comply with the terms of the subpoena issued on the 23rd of October, 2012, under which he was ordered to appear testify in this case. The Chamber accordingly orders that Mr. Krstic appear for testimony in this case on Monday, 25th of March, 2013. The Chamber instructs the Registry to take the necessary measures in relation thereto and to communicate this ruling to Mr. Krstic and his legal representatives. The Chamber reiterates that the wilful failure to comply with the terms of a subpoena constitutes contempt of the Tribunal pursuant to Rule 77 of the Rules which is punishable by a term of imprisonment not exceeding seven years and a fine not exceeding 100.000 euros, or both. Next matter is related to Witness Puhalic. In assessing the accused's motion for subpoena to Slavko Puhalic filed on the 1st of March, 2013, the Chamber has noted that in the declaration attached as confidential annex A to the motion, the accused's case manager refers to a different last name for the witness as well as a different Rule 65 ter number for the witness statement provided to the Defence team than those referred to in the motion. The Chamber notes that the 65 ter number provided in the declaration pertains to a statement for another witness who has already testified in this case. Therefore, if Mr. Robinson could take a look into the issue and inform the Chamber the result by tomorrow. The last matter is related to Witness Milan Martic. The Chamber has received the witness list for the next week already, and there, again, Mr. Milan Martic is not there. So given that the Chamber ordered that a week would be sufficient for the witness for the purpose of proofing and else, so Chamber expresses its concern about his testimony being delayed. So I would -- I would expect Milan Martic's evidence to be heard immediately following Mr. Krstic's evidence in the week of 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't want to take up the time after the recess but for some reasons that probably won't -- may not be possible. Would you like to hear that now or should I submit that to you in writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informally informed that there are some issues as regards the counsel, but whatever the reasoning might be, I think the 25th of March -- the week of 25th would be more than sufficient for him to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we -- we haven't had any proofing with him and we aren't able to start any proofing until he obtains the counsel which is a matter between -- now between him and the Registry, and I understand he is going to ask the Chamber to make a ruling on that. And then the Prosecution, I know, would like to receive adequate time after receiving the Rule 92 ter statement before it begins its cross-examination. So I'd -- I really don't think that that's practicable given the situation but we can explore that further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All can I say at the moment, given -- in light of the Chamber's interest, there would be some development in that regard. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.48 p.m.,
